---
pagetitle: "From mutualism to parasitism: ant-interaction strategy, partner breadth and range size in lycaenid butterflies"
bibliography: lycaenidae_references.bib
link-citations: true
# RStudio's Knit button: render Word and HTML next to this file, then apply the Word table layout (column widths,
# fonts, spacing) exactly as code/render_report.R does; without it Word stretches table columns unevenly.
knit: (function(input, ...) { out <- rmarkdown::render(input, output_format = "all", envir = new.env(parent = globalenv())); source(file.path(dirname(normalizePath(input)), "..", "code", "R", "docx_layout.R")); for (f in out[grepl("[.]docx$", out)]) finalise_publication_docx(f); invisible(out) })
output:
  bookdown::word_document2:
    reference_docx: docx_template.docx
    fig_caption: true
    global_numbering: true
    pandoc_args: ["--lua-filter=caption_style.lua"]
    toc: false
  bookdown::html_document2:
    fig_caption: true
    global_numbering: true
    number_sections: true
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
---

options(report_table_width = 6.5, report_table_layouts = list()) # layouts registered for finalise_publication_docx()

# All results are read from the notebook folders in data/intermediate, written by the notebooks
# code/s02_prepare_ranges.Rmd to code/s06_summarise_results.Rmd; figures come from results/.
dir_s02 <- resrepo::path_resrepo("data/intermediate/s02_prepare_ranges")        # record counts, outlier-rule check
dir_s03 <- resrepo::path_resrepo("data/intermediate/s03_build_species_tables")  # analysis species tables
dir_s04 <- resrepo::path_resrepo("data/intermediate/s04_fit_models")            # main models and phylogenetic models
dir_s05 <- resrepo::path_resrepo("data/intermediate/s05_check_robustness")      # robustness checks
dir_s06 <- resrepo::path_resrepo("data/intermediate/s06_summarise_results")     # report and supplement tables
main_models <- read_report_rds(file.path(dir_s04, "main_models.rds"))
main <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "main_coefficients.csv"))
contrasts <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "main_contrasts.csv"))
main_means <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "main_estimated_means.csv"))
main_metadata <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "main_metadata.csv"))
dir_checks <- dir_s05
check_table <- function(name) read_report_table(file.path(dir_checks, paste0(name, ".csv")))
within_breadth <- check_table("breadth_within_strategy")
rare_results <- check_table("rarefied_models")
regional_results <- check_table("regional_and_pair_omissions")
# one regional comparison (s05_check_robustness, Regions and genera; Table S13c)
reg_row <- function(subset, model = "lmm", tree = NA_character_, contrast = "f-p", measure = "area") {
  x <- regional_results
  d <- x[x$subset == subset & x$dropped == "none" & x$model == model & x$contrast == contrast &
    x$measure == measure & (if (is.na(tree)) is.na(x$tree) else x$tree %in% tree), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
pair_genus <- check_table("genus_pair_omission")
matched_checks <- check_table("matched_sample_contrasts")
matched_checks_metadata <- check_table("matched_sample_metadata")
# one range-area type contrast of the tree-matched sample: model "pgls" or "matched_lmm"
mcv <- function(model, contrast, tree) {
  d <- matched_checks[matched_checks$model == model & gsub(" ", "", matched_checks$contrast) == contrast &
                        matched_checks$study == tree & matched_checks$measure == "area" &
                        matched_checks$predictors == "type", ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
cleaning_results <- check_table("cleaning_contrasts")
cleaning_expert <- check_table("cleaning_expert_validation")
# Discussion 5.1 and Appendix S5: minimum number of origins of parasitism by parsimony on the
# genus-grafted and matched-only trees (s05_check_robustness, Origins of parasitism); orig("schar_2018")$min_origins = "16"
origins <- check_table("parasitism_origins")
origin_clades <- check_table("parasitism_origin_clades")
orig <- function(tree, tips = "grafted") {
  x <- origins[origins$tree == tree & origins$tips == tips, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1L)
  x
}
# "Both trees required N changes, all of them origins": on every tree the fewest and most gains among the most
# parsimonious reconstructions equal the number of changes, so none includes a loss
stopifnot(nrow(origins) == 4L, all(origins$min_origins == origins$changes), all(origins$max_origins == origins$changes),
          orig("yumnam_2025")$changes == orig("schar_2018")$changes,
          nrow(origin_clades) == 2L * orig("schar_2018")$changes)
origin_singles <- sort(origin_clades$genera[origin_clades$tree == "schar_2018" & origin_clades$n_species == 1L])
# Results 4.1: parasites formed "the highest proportions" of classified species in southern Africa (Fig. 1D):
# the three cells with the highest parasite share (cells with >= 10 classified species, as mapped) lie in the
# southern Africa region of Appendix S5 (latitude < -15, 10 < longitude < 55)
local({
  cells <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s06, "interaction_cells_500km.csv"))
  cells <- cells[cells$n_classified >= 10, ]
  top <- head(cells[order(-cells$prop_parasitic), ], 3)
  stopifnot(nrow(top) == 3L, all(top$cell_latitude < -15 & top$cell_longitude > 10 & top$cell_longitude < 55))
})
# Appendix S5, "Matched species, lineages and regions": each claim of the paragraph, range area
local({
  rp_ <- function(subset, model, tree, contrast, dropped = "none") {
    x <- regional_results[regional_results$subset == subset & regional_results$dropped == dropped &
      regional_results$model == model & regional_results$contrast == contrast & regional_results$measure == "area" &
      (if (is.na(tree)) is.na(regional_results$tree) | regional_results$tree == "" else regional_results$tree %in% tree), ]
    stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1L)
    x$p
  }
  gp_ <- function(tree, contrast) {
    x <- pair_genus[pair_genus$tree == tree & pair_genus$contrast == contrast & pair_genus$measure == "area", ]
    stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1L)
    x$p
  }
  lt <- "Lepidochrysops + Thestor"
  # tree-matched species: f-p supported in PGLS and in the taxonomic model of the same species on both trees;
  # n-p supported in the taxonomic model but not in PGLS
  mc_ <- matched_checks[matched_checks$measure == "area" & matched_checks$predictors == "type" &
                          gsub(" ", "", matched_checks$contrast) %in% c("f-p", "n-p"), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(mc_) == 8L, all(mc_$p.value[gsub(" ", "", mc_$contrast) == "f-p"] < 0.05),
            all(mc_$p.value[mc_$model == "matched_lmm"] < 0.05),
            all(mc_$p.value[mc_$model == "pgls" & gsub(" ", "", mc_$contrast) == "n-p"] >= 0.05))
  # without Lepidochrysops and Thestor: f-p supported except in species-level Yumnam PGLS
  stopifnot(rp_("all", "lmm", NA, "f-p", lt) < 0.05, rp_("all", "pgls", "schar_2018", "f-p", lt) < 0.05,
            rp_("all", "pgls", "yumnam_2025", "f-p", lt) >= 0.05,
            gp_("yumnam_2025", "f-p") < 0.05, gp_("schar_2018", "f-p") < 0.05)
  # ... n-p supported only in genus-by-type PGLS on the Schar tree
  stopifnot(rp_("all", "lmm", NA, "n-p", lt) >= 0.05, rp_("all", "pgls", "yumnam_2025", "n-p", lt) >= 0.05,
            rp_("all", "pgls", "schar_2018", "n-p", lt) >= 0.05, gp_("yumnam_2025", "n-p") >= 0.05,
            gp_("schar_2018", "n-p") < 0.05)
  # southern Africa only: f-p and n-p supported, m-p not, in all three models
  for (m in list(c("lmm", NA), c("pgls", "yumnam_2025"), c("pgls", "schar_2018")))
    stopifnot(rp_("southern_Africa_only", m[1], m[2], "f-p") < 0.05, rp_("southern_Africa_only", m[1], m[2], "n-p") < 0.05,
              rp_("southern_Africa_only", m[1], m[2], "m-p") >= 0.05)
  # ... and mutualists had smaller ranges than facultative species in all three models
  for (m in list(c("lmm", NA), c("pgls", "yumnam_2025"), c("pgls", "schar_2018")))
    stopifnot(rp_("southern_Africa_only", m[1], m[2], "f-m") < 0.05)
  # outside southern Africa: f-p supported in the taxonomic model and on the Schar tree, not on the Yumnam tree;
  # n-p supported only on the Schar tree
  stopifnot(rp_("excluding_southern_Africa", "lmm", NA, "f-p") < 0.05,
            rp_("excluding_southern_Africa", "pgls", "schar_2018", "f-p") < 0.05,
            rp_("excluding_southern_Africa", "pgls", "yumnam_2025", "f-p") >= 0.05,
            rp_("excluding_southern_Africa", "lmm", NA, "n-p") >= 0.05,
            rp_("excluding_southern_Africa", "pgls", "yumnam_2025", "n-p") >= 0.05,
            rp_("excluding_southern_Africa", "pgls", "schar_2018", "n-p") < 0.05)
})
dir_boxcox <- dir_s05
boxcox_comparison <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_boxcox, "boxcox_comparison.csv"))
boxcox_powers <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_boxcox, "boxcox_powers.csv"))
bc_power_text <- function(key) {
  value <- boxcox_powers$lambda[boxcox_powers$model == key]
  stopifnot(length(value) == 1L, is.finite(value))
  report_number(value, 3)
}
cell_ci <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f) %s", x$ratio, x$lower, x$upper, format_table_p(x$p))
within_eff <- function(model, measure = "area") {
  x <- within_breadth[within_breadth$model == model & within_breadth$measure == measure, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1L)
  num <- function(v) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", v), fixed = TRUE) # true minus sign (U+2212)
  lower <- 100 * (x$lower - 1)
  # "to" between the bounds when the lower bound is negative
  sprintf(
    "%s%% (95%% CI %s%s%s%%; %s)", num(100 * (x$ratio - 1)), num(lower),
    if (lower < 0) " to " else "–", num(100 * (x$upper - 1)), fmt_p(x$p)
  )
}
robust <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s06, "robustness.csv"))
# Two further rows of the core results, transformed as in s06_summarise_results, Robustness table (facultative /
# non-associated shown as f-n): rarefied ranges (ten random localities per species, s05_check_robustness, Models on rarefied ranges), a core
# analysis of Figure 4 (s06_summarise_results, Figures 4 and S8); and PGLS + butterfly background
# (s04_fit_models, Joint phylogenetic and spatial models).
as_robust_rows <- function(x, analysis) {
  x$contrast <- gsub(" ", "", x$contrast)
  flip <- x$contrast == "n-f"
  x[flip, c("ratio", "lower", "upper")] <- 1 / x[flip, c("ratio", "upper", "lower")]
  x$contrast[flip] <- "f-n"
  x$analysis <- analysis
  x <- x[intersect(names(robust), names(x))]
  for (column in setdiff(names(robust), names(x))) x[[column]] <- NA
  x[names(robust)]
}

robust <- rbind(robust, as_robust_rows(rare_core, "rarefied_k10"),

# one verified value per call; ambiguity stops the knit
cnt <- function(name, digits = 0L) {
  v <- counts$value[counts$name == name]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  report_number(v, digits)
}
rb <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- robust[robust$analysis == analysis & robust$contrast == contrast & robust$measure == measure, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else paste0("p = ", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
# larval carnivory check (s05_check_robustness, Larval carnivory; Discussion 5.1, Appendix S6): counts in the main range-area
# sample and plant-feeder / carnivore ratios among non-parasites (ratios below one: larger carnivore ranges)
carn_counts <- check_table("carnivory_counts")
carn_check <- check_table("carnivory_check")
carn_n <- function(type = c("n", "f", "m", "p"), carnivory = c("plant", "animal", "uncoded"),
                   basis = c("species", "genus", "none"))
  sum(carn_counts$n[carn_counts$interaction_type %in% type & carn_counts$carnivory %in% carnivory &
                      carn_counts$basis %in% basis])
carn_row <- function(analysis, measure = "area") {
  d <- carn_check[carn_check$analysis == analysis & carn_check$measure == measure, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
carn_eff <- function(analysis, measure = "area") {
  d <- carn_row(analysis, measure)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f, 95%% CI %.2f–%.2f, %s", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
local({
  coded <- carn_row("coded")
  # "no analysed parasite was coded as a plant feeder"; the sample is the main range-area sample
  stopifnot(carn_n("p", "plant") == 0L, carn_n() == counts$value[counts$name == "model_area_type_total"],
            carn_n("p") == counts$value[counts$name == "model_area_type_p"])
  # "mostly hemipteran-feeding Miletinae"; counts agree with the model sample
  stopifnot(coded$n_carnivore == carn_n(c("n", "f", "m"), "animal"), coded$n_carnivore_miletinae > coded$n_carnivore / 2)
  # Appendix S6: "one subfamily, which contains no plant feeders"; "only four carnivores remained" (num_word)
  stopifnot(coded$n_plant_miletinae == 0L, carn_row("without_miletinae")$n_carnivore <= 10L)
  # "did not have smaller ranges than plant feeders": no supported difference and point estimates favour carnivores
  stopifnot(all(carn_check$p >= 0.05), all(carn_check$ratio < 1))
})
eff <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, contrast, measure)
  sprintf("%.2f (95%% CI %.2f–%.2f; %s)", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
# inside brackets: "ratio 1.55, 95% CI 0.87-2.76, p = 0.198"
effi <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, contrast, measure)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f, 95%% CI %.2f–%.2f, %s", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
# inside brackets, one decimal, no p-value (abstract): "ratio 2.4, 95% CI 1.2-4.9"
effi_short <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, contrast, measure)
  stopifnot(d$lower > 1 || d$upper < 1)  # the interval alone must show the contrast is supported
  sprintf("ratio %.1f, 95%% CI %.1f–%.1f", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper)
}
# running text: "10.0-fold (95% CI 3.3-30.3; p < 0.001)"
fold <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, contrast, measure)
  sprintf("%.1f-fold (95%% CI %.1f–%.1f; %s)", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
ratio <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area", digits = 1L) report_number(rb(analysis, contrast, measure)$ratio, digits)
# running text after a ratio: "95% CI 3.6–36.4; p < 0.001"
ci_p <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, contrast, measure)
  sprintf("95%% CI %.1f–%.1f; %s", d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
pct <- function(analysis, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, "breadth", measure)
  sprintf("%.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f–%.1f%%; %s)", 100 * (d$ratio - 1), 100 * (d$lower - 1), 100 * (d$upper - 1), fmt_p(d$p))
}
mor <- function(model, km) {
  v <- moran$moran_i[moran$model == model & moran$distance_km == km]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  sub("^-", "−", report_number(v, 2))  # typographic minus for negative Moran's I
}
pg <- function(column, study = "yumnam_2025", measure = "area", predictors = "type", tree_set = "grafted") {
  v <- pgls_metadata[[column]][pgls_metadata$study == study & pgls_metadata$measure == measure &
    pgls_metadata$predictors == predictors & pgls_metadata$tree_set == tree_set]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  v
}
pgls_coverage <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "pgls_grafted_coverage.csv"))
pgc <- function(column, study = "yumnam_2025") {
  v <- pgls_coverage[[column]][pgls_coverage$study == study]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  report_number(v)
}
daru_parasites <- sum(daru_table$interaction_type %in% "p" & is.finite(daru_table$range_area) &
  daru_table$range_area > 0)
# rows of the all-results table (Table S12), in the order of the report

analysis_labels <- c(
  lmm = "Taxonomic mixed model (main)", spherical_gam = "Spherical spatial GAM",
  background_500km_butterflies = "Mixed model + butterfly regional background",
  pgls_grafted_yumnam_2025 = "PGLS, species level, Yumnam tree", pgls_grafted_schar_2018 = "PGLS, species level, Schär tree",
  pgls_yumnam_2025 = "PGLS, matched species, Yumnam tree", pgls_schar_2018 = "PGLS, matched species, Schär tree",
  phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025 = "Phylogenetic spatial GAM, Yumnam tree",
  phylo_spatial_schar_2018 = "Phylogenetic spatial GAM, Schär tree",
  pgls_background_yumnam_2025 = "PGLS + butterfly regional background, Yumnam tree",
  pgls_background_schar_2018 = "PGLS + butterfly regional background, Schär tree",
  pgls_genus_yumnam_2025 = "PGLS, genus level, Yumnam tree", pgls_genus_schar_2018 = "PGLS, genus level, Schär tree",
  rarefied_k10 = "Rarefied ranges (ten localities)",
  modelled_ranges_daru = "Modelled ranges (Daru)",
  stability_80 = "80% range-stability subset",
  stability_90 = "90% range-stability subset", stability_95 = "95% range-stability subset",
  wingspan_covariate = "Wingspan as covariate"
)
# the core analyses of main-text Figure 4: the main model, the spatial GAM, the three phylogenetic
# analyses on both trees, rarefied ranges and modelled ranges
core_analyses <- c("lmm", "spherical_gam", "pgls_grafted_yumnam_2025", "pgls_grafted_schar_2018",
  "phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025", "phylo_spatial_schar_2018", "pgls_genus_yumnam_2025", "pgls_genus_schar_2018",
  "rarefied_k10", "modelled_ranges_daru")
core_ratio <- function(contrast) vapply(core_analyses, function(a) rb(a, contrast)$ratio, 1)
core_p <- function(contrast) vapply(core_analyses, function(a) rb(a, contrast)$p, 1)
# number of core analyses with p < 0.05 for a range-area contrast: "all ten" or "nine of the ten"
core_support <- function(contrast) {
  k <- sum(core_p(contrast) < 0.05)
  n <- length(core_analyses)
  if (k == n) paste("all", num_word(n)) else paste(num_word(k), "of the", num_word(n))
}
# range of a range-area contrast across the core analyses, e.g. "2.4–14.5"
span <- function(contrast = "f-p") sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", min(core_ratio(contrast)), max(core_ratio(contrast)))
# the same range over the supporting core analyses only (Results 4.4: "nine of the ten (ratios …)")
span_supported <- function(contrast) {
  r <- core_ratio(contrast)[core_p(contrast) < 0.05]
  sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", min(r), max(r))
}
# Abstract: breadth "supported in every core analysis estimating it" (genus-level PGLS has no breadth)
local({
  b <- robust[robust$measure == "area" & robust$contrast == "breadth" & robust$analysis %in% core_analyses, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(b) >= 7L, all(b$p < 0.05), !any(grepl("pgls_genus", b$analysis)))
})
# number of supporting core analyses as a word, e.g. "five"
core_k <- function(contrast) num_word(sum(core_p(contrast) < 0.05))
# Discussion 5.2: "Parasites had smaller estimated ranges than mutualists in every core analysis"
stopifnot(all(core_ratio("m-p") > 1))
# Conclusions: obligate parasites "consistently had the smallest ranges" (every core point estimate below the other types)
stopifnot(all(core_ratio("f-p") > 1), all(core_ratio("n-p") > 1))
# Discussion 5.3: the breadth association "held in every analysis, including spatial, phylogenetic,
# rarefied-range and modelled-range models" (positive and p < 0.05 in every range-area analysis estimating it)
local({
  b <- robust[robust$contrast == "breadth" & robust$measure == "area", ]
  stopifnot(all(c("spherical_gam", "pgls_grafted_yumnam_2025", "pgls_grafted_schar_2018", "phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025",
    "phylo_spatial_schar_2018", "rarefied_k10", "modelled_ranges_daru") %in% b$analysis), all(b$ratio > 1), all(b$p < 0.05))
})
# ratio and p only (running text): "ratio 2.08, p = 0.078"
rp <- function(analysis, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- rb(analysis, contrast, measure)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f, %s", d$ratio, fmt_p(d$p))
}
# genus-level PGLS (s04_fit_models, Genus-level PGLS)
glev <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "genus_level_pgls.csv"))
# Appendix S5: genus-by-type PGLS, range area, all genera: m-p and f-m "supported only on the Schär tree"
gl_check <- function() {
  g <- glev[glev$measure == "area" & glev$dropped == "none" & gsub(" ", "", glev$contrast) %in% c("m-p", "f-m"), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(g) == 4L, all(g$p[g$tree == "schar_2018"] < 0.05), all(g$p[g$tree == "yumnam_2025"] >= 0.05))
}
gl_check()
gl <- function(tree, dropped = "none", contrast = "f-p", measure = "area") {
  d <- glev[glev$tree == tree & glev$dropped == dropped & glev$contrast == contrast & glev$measure == measure, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
# Appendix S5: genus-level lambda "close to zero on the Schar tree" (range area, all genera)
stopifnot(gl("schar_2018")$lambda < 0.05)
gli <- function(tree, dropped = "none", contrast = "f-p", measure = "area") {
  d <- gl(tree, dropped, contrast, measure)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f, 95%% CI %.2f–%.2f, %s", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
# leave-parasitic-genus-out check (s04_fit_models, Leave-one-genus-out)
logo <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "leave_genus_out.csv"))
lg <- function(dropped, model, contrast = "f-p") {
  d <- logo[logo$dropped == dropped & logo$model == model & logo$contrast == contrast, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
# ratio and p only (running text)
lg_rp <- function(dropped, model, contrast = "f-p") {
  d <- lg(dropped, model, contrast)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f, %s", d$ratio, fmt_p(d$p))
}
stopifnot(!any(grepl(" + ", logo$dropped, fixed = TRUE))) # single-genus omissions only
logo_single <- setdiff(unique(logo$dropped), "none")
# parasites of an omitted genus in the main LMM sample = parasites of the full model minus those left
n_par_genus <- function(g) lg("none", "lmm")$n_parasite - lg(g, "lmm")$n_parasite
# Scientific patterns are audited against the rendered text; significance is not a render prerequisite.
n_mp_lost <- sum(logo$p[logo$model == "lmm" & logo$contrast == "m-p" & logo$dropped %in% logo_single] >= 0.05)
# counts up to ten as words, larger counts as digits
num_word <- function(k) {
  stopifnot(length(k) == 1L, k >= 0, k == round(k))
  if (k > 10) return(as.character(k))
  c("none", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")[k + 1L]
}
# median recorded breadth by type in the area breadth model (raw counts recovered from the centred predictor, as in
# s06_summarise_results, Figure 3; Results 4.3): "median two versus one genus" requires equal mutualist and parasite medians
breadth_med <- local({
  b <- model.frame(main_models$area_breadth)
  centre <- main_metadata$partner_breadth_mean[main_metadata$measure == "area" & main_metadata$predictors == "breadth"]
  stopifnot(length(centre) == 1L)
  raw <- b$partner_breadth_centered + centre
  stopifnot(all(abs(raw - round(raw)) < 1e-8))
  med <- tapply(round(raw), b$interaction_type, median)
  stopifnot(all(med[c("f", "m", "p")] == round(med[c("f", "m", "p")])), med[["m"]] == med[["p"]])
  med
})
# the Afro-Eurasia and Australasia subset (data key Old_World_only; longitude >= -30) keeps every analysed parasite,
# including the Australasian ones (Results 4.4)
stopifnot(reg_row("Old_World_only")$n_parasite == counts$value[counts$name == "model_area_type_p"])
# Abstract: the most conservative facultative-parasite estimate (smallest core ratio) is the Yumnam joint
# model, and it is the only core analysis without support for the non-associated-parasite contrast ("the most
# conservative, a joint spatial–phylogenetic model" and "the other nine")
stopifnot(names(which.min(core_ratio("f-p"))) == "phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025",
          identical(unname(core_analyses[core_p("n-p") >= 0.05]), "phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025"))
# evidence-database scale (s06_summarise_results, Supporting Information tables): Abstract and Appendix S1
si_ledger <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s06, "si_ledger_summary.csv"))
ledger_n <- function(k) {
  v <- si_ledger[[k]]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  v
}
```

Lycaenidae. *Upper panel*, from left: *Phengaris arion* (obligate parasite),
larva among *Myrmica sabuleti* workers and brood; *Jalmenus evagoras* (obligate
mutualist), larva attended by *Iridomyrmex mayri* on *Acacia dealbata*;
*Lycaena phlaeas* (not ant-associated), larva on *Rumex acetosella*; and
*Plebejus* (*Lycaeides*) *melissa* (facultative associate), larva attended by *Formica aerata*
on *Medicago sativa*. The blue arrow orders the interaction types by estimated
range size: obligate parasites had the smallest estimates, facultative
associates usually the largest, and obligate mutualists and non-associated
species were intermediate and did not differ clearly from each other. The
clearest contrast was between facultative associates and parasites, and
contrasts involving mutualists were less consistent across analyses.
*Lower panel:* ranges were larger in species with more recorded
ant genera, represented by a single *M. sabuleti* worker (left) and workers of
*Camponotus japonicus*, *Crematogaster scutellaris*, *M. sabuleti* and
*Oecophylla smaragdina* (right). The species shown are examples, not data
points; arrows show direction only; and only the four workers on the right
share a common scale. Illustrations were generated
with ChatGPT and carefully revised against photographic and taxonomic references.

# Abstract

**Aim.** Biotic interactions can limit or extend species distributions, but how
interaction strategies spanning mutualism and parasitism relate to range size
remains poorly understood. We tested whether ant-interaction strategy and
recorded ant-partner breadth are associated with range size across Lycaenidae.

**Location.** Global.

**Time period.** 1900–2026.

**Major taxa studied.** Lycaenidae butterflies and associated ants
(Formicidae).

**Methods.** We compiled a family-wide dataset of lycaenid–ant interactions
(`r report_number(ledger_n("claims"))` published records for
`r report_number(ledger_n("species"))` species, each linked to its source),
classified species into four interaction strategies and estimated range area and
latitudinal and longitudinal extents from cleaned occurrences. Taxonomic mixed
models related range size to interaction strategy and the number of recorded ant
genera. We tested robustness with `r num_word(length(core_analyses))` core
analyses addressing spatial and phylogenetic non-independence, parasite
concentration in a few genera, occurrence sampling and range estimation.

**Results.** Across `r cnt("model_area_type_total")` species, estimated range
area was smallest in obligate parasites, intermediate in obligate mutualists and
largest in facultative associates (`r ratio("lmm", "f-p")` times that of
parasites) and non-associated species (`r ratio("lmm", "n-p")` times), which did
not differ clearly from each other. The facultative–parasite contrast was
supported in `r core_support("f-p")` core analyses, including the most
conservative, a joint spatial–phylogenetic model
(`r effi_short("phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025", "f-p")`), and the
non-associated–parasite contrast in the other `r core_k("n-p")`. Mutualist
contrasts were model-dependent. Each additional recorded ant genus was
associated with `r report_number(100 * (rb("lmm", "breadth")$ratio - 1), 0)`%
greater range area (supported in every core analysis estimating it).
Interaction type explained
`r report_number(100 * main_metadata$marginal_r2[main_metadata$measure == "area" & main_metadata$predictors == "type"], 1)`%
of range-area variation, and type with breadth
`r report_number(100 * main_metadata$marginal_r2[main_metadata$measure == "area" & main_metadata$predictors == "breadth"], 1)`%
among species with recorded partners (marginal R²).

**Main conclusions.** Range size varied with how, rather than whether, species
interact with ants, with small ranges linked to obligate parasitism. The breadth
association is consistent with the niche-breadth hypothesis, although
documentation effort and geographic opportunity offer alternative explanations.
Range-size studies should consider the type of biotic interaction alongside
environmental and resource niches.

**Keywords.** Biotic interactions; biotic niche; Formicidae; geographic range
size; Lycaenidae; macroecology; mutualism; myrmecophily; niche breadth;
parasitism.

# Introduction

Geographic range size varies by several orders of magnitude among species, and
understanding its determinants is a central goal in ecology and biogeography
[@brown1996; @gaston2009], not least because range size is closely linked to
extinction risk [@chichorro2019]. Range size reflects ecological tolerances, the
geographic availability of suitable conditions and resources, dispersal,
evolutionary history and biotic interactions [@sheth2020]. Among its most
consistently supported correlates is niche breadth: species with broader
environmental tolerances or habitat and resource use generally occupy larger
ranges [@brown1984; @slatyer2013]. Dispersal and historical opportunity further
affect how much of the potential distribution a species reaches [@alzate2022].
Biotic interactions, however, remain much less integrated into comparative
explanations of range size than climate, habitat and resource use
[@paquette2021; @thuiller2023; @galiana2026].

Biotic interactions—the Eltonian dimension of species' niches—can limit and
extend distributions. Competition, predation and parasitism can prevent
populations from persisting, whereas mutualists can allow species to occupy
otherwise unsuitable conditions [@wisz2013; @afkhami2014; @paquette2021].
Evidence that interactions contribute to individual range boundaries is
substantial [@louthan2015; @paquette2021], and interactions can constrain
range expansion over evolutionary time [@pigot2013]. Total range size, unlike
range limits, integrates processes at multiple boundaries, across heterogeneous
environments and over long periods of colonisation and extinction, so
interactions are often assumed to matter less at this scale [@galiana2023]. Yet
in gall-inducing sawflies and their parasitoids, larger ranges were associated
with wider climatic tolerances and more trophic interactions, and diet breadth
appeared more limiting than climatic tolerance [@galiana2023].
Interaction types are usually studied in isolation, so little is known about
whether contrasting interaction strategies leave predictable range-size
signatures.

Interaction strategies differ along two axes that may affect range size: how
strongly a species depends on its partners, and whether it benefits them or
exploits them. Facultative mutualists benefit from partners where present
but can persist without them. Obligate mutualists gain similar benefits but also
depend on compatible partners, which can restrict them to the geographic overlap
of their own and their partners' environmental requirements [@fowler2022].
Consistent with this trade-off, facultative positive interactions tend to extend
geographic or ecological ranges, whereas obligate ones more often constrain them
[@stephan2021]. Obligate parasites share this dependence but also exploit their hosts. They may therefore need large host colonies or dense host populations
[@thomas1992; @tsai2010], and the harm they cause can select for host defences that make exploitation vary geographically [@nash2008].

A third axis, partner breadth, may modify these constraints, extending the
niche-breadth hypothesis to the biotic niche. Species able to use more partners should find
suitable ones in more places. Consistent with this, legumes and ants with more
generalised mutualisms are more likely to have established beyond their native
ranges [@harrison2018; @nathan2023], and more host-specific fleas have smaller
geographic ranges [@krasnov2005]. Such correlations can also run the other way,
because wide-ranging species may encounter more potential partners simply by
occurring in more places [@hurtado2024]. Causality therefore remains hard to
establish.

Lycaenid butterflies (Lycaenidae) are particularly well suited to testing these
ideas. Within this single family, interaction strategies span a spectrum from no
ant association through facultative and obligate mutualism to obligate
parasitism, so strategies can be compared among related species with broadly
similar life cycles.
More than 70% of almost 5,400 species worldwide appear to be ant-associated when
known life histories are extrapolated across close relatives [@pierce2002;
@piercedankowicz2022a]. Mutualistically associated larvae commonly provide
nutritive secretions and receive protection from ants, which can substantially
increase larval survival. In *Plebejus* (*Lycaeides*) *melissa*, ant attendance
increases survival on a suboptimal host plant [@forister2010]. Parasitic
species instead obtain food from ant brood or through trophallaxis
(mouth-to-mouth feeding by ants), often relying on specialised chemical or
behavioural mechanisms to enter and persist within colonies [@pierce2002].

Lycaenidae also stood out in a recent comparison of niche breadth and range size.
Across
European-centred butterflies, climatic niche breadth was the strongest predictor
of range size, whereas relationships with habitat and diet breadth differed
substantially among lineages [@hausharter2023]. In Lycaenidae, range size
increased with climatic and habitat breadth but mostly decreased with larval
plant-diet breadth, which the authors suggested might reflect ant associations
as an additional niche dimension. Within the family, ecological specialisation is
associated with stronger genetic structure, and ant associations add a further
dimension to that specialisation [@schar2018]. The ant-associated niche may
therefore capture range-size
variation that climate, habitat and larval host plants do not. To our knowledge,
however, whether ant-interaction strategy and recorded partner breadth are
associated with range size remains untested across the family.

We hypothesised that (1) facultatively
associated species would have relatively large ranges, because they can gain
benefits from ants without strict dependence; (2) obligate mutualists would have
smaller ranges than facultative and non-associated species, because persistence
additionally requires compatible ants, although mutualistic benefits could
partly offset this constraint; (3) obligate parasites would have the smallest
ranges, because ant dependence is combined with specialised exploitation that
harms their hosts; and (4) range size would increase with the number of recorded
ant genera, consistent with the niche-breadth hypothesis. We tested them with a
new source-traceable global compilation of Lycaenidae–ant associations and
cleaned occurrence records. Obligate associations are concentrated in particular
regions, notably Australia and southern Africa, largely because lineages rich in
obligate associates occur there [@pierce2002]. Because interaction
strategies and range sizes are geographically and phylogenetically structured,
we evaluated whether these associations were robust to spatial and phylogenetic
non-independence, as well as to the concentration of parasites in a few genera,
occurrence sampling and range estimation.

```{r setup-supplement, include=FALSE}
# Supporting Information inputs (s04_fit_models, Joint phylogenetic and spatial models; s06_summarise_results, Supporting Information tables)
si <- function(name) read_report_table(file.path(dir_s06, paste0("si_", name, ".csv")))
si_evidence <- si("evidence_basis")
si_attrition <- si("attrition")
si_alternative <- si("alternative_decisions")
# facultative-parasite area ratios after inclusive cleaning (eligible and identical samples) and with species-level
# subtype evidence only: the two decisions that "roughly halved" the main ratio (Results 4.4)
halved_fp <- c(
  cleaning_results$ratio[cleaning_results$measure == "area" & cleaning_results$predictors == "type" &
    cleaning_results$contrast == "f-p" & cleaning_results$cleaning == "inclusive"],
  si_alternative$ratio[si_alternative$measure == "area" & si_alternative$contrast == "f-p" &
    si_alternative$decision == "species_level_subtype_only"])
stopifnot(length(halved_fp) == 3L, all(halved_fp / rb("lmm", "f-p")$ratio > 0.4 & halved_fp / rb("lmm", "f-p")$ratio < 0.65))
halved_fp_span <- sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", min(halved_fp), max(halved_fp))
# Discussion opening: facultative associates are "the majority of ant-associated species"
stopifnot(counts$value[counts$name == "model_area_type_f"] >
  counts$value[counts$name == "model_area_type_m"] + counts$value[counts$name == "model_area_type_p"])
# Results 4.4: facultative associates "had clearly larger ranges than parasites under every alternative range estimate" and "(all supported)" in the
# 80%, 90% and 95% stability subsets
stopifnot(all(vapply(c("rarefied_k10", "modelled_ranges_daru", "stability_80", "stability_90", "stability_95"),
                     function(a) rb(a, "f-p")$p < 0.05 && rb(a, "f-p")$ratio > 1, TRUE)))
# Discussion: within southern Africa both parasite contrasts have "larger ratios than in the full sample" in all
# three models, and "both parasite contrasts also held with rarefied, modelled and differently cleaned ranges"
for (m in list(c("lmm", NA, "lmm"), c("pgls", "yumnam_2025", "pgls_grafted_yumnam_2025"),
               c("pgls", "schar_2018", "pgls_grafted_schar_2018")))
  for (k in c("f-p", "n-p"))
    stopifnot(reg_row("southern_Africa_only", m[1], m[2], k)$ratio > rb(m[3], k)$ratio)
stopifnot(all(vapply(c("rarefied_k10", "modelled_ranges_daru"),
                     function(a) rb(a, "n-p")$p < 0.05 && rb(a, "n-p")$ratio > 1, TRUE)),
          with(cleaning_results[cleaning_results$measure == "area" & cleaning_results$predictors == "type" &
                                  cleaning_results$contrast %in% c("f-p", "n-p"), ], all(p < 0.05 & ratio > 1)))
si_contamination <- si("background_contamination")
si_expert <- si("expert_validation")
si_overlay <- si("phylogeny_overlay_counts")
# dataset summaries (s06_summarise_results, Supporting Information tables): agreement with the earlier manual
# compilation, classification coverage by region, sample composition of the alternative codings
legacy <- si("legacy_agreement")
stopifnot(nrow(legacy) == 1L)
coverage <- si("classification_coverage")
cov_row <- function(region) {
  x <- coverage[coverage$region == region, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1L)
  x
}
alt_counts <- si("alternative_counts")
alt_n <- function(decision, column) {
  v <- alt_counts[[column]][alt_counts$decision == decision]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  v
}
# analysed mutualists or parasites whose subtype rests on a genus statement or a source's inference from
# relatives (basis other than 'direct'): those dropped by the species-level-only decision (Appendices S1, S6)
main_table <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s03, "species_table.csv"))
main_table <- main_table[!is.na(main_table$interaction_type) & is.finite(main_table$range_area) &
                           main_table$range_area > 0 & !is.na(main_table$genus) & !is.na(main_table$subfamily), ]
subtype_indirect <- function(type) {
  indirect <- main_table$interaction_type %in% type & !main_table$interaction_type_basis %in% "direct"
  v <- sum(indirect)
  col <- paste0("n_", type)
  stopifnot(v == alt_n("main", col) - alt_n("species_level_subtype_only", col))
  # "mainly Lepidochrysops and Thestor" (Appendix S1) holds only for the parasites
  if (type == "p") stopifnot(sum(main_table$genus[indirect] %in% c("Lepidochrysops", "Thestor")) > v / 2)
  v
}
# of these, analysed mutualists or parasites whose obligate association was documented for the species (basis
# 'direct_class_inferred_subtype'), which Table S1 therefore counts as species-specific (Appendix S1)
subtype_added <- function(type) {
  v <- sum(main_table$interaction_type %in% type & main_table$interaction_type_basis %in% "direct_class_inferred_subtype")
  stopifnot(v + sum(si_evidence[[type]][si_evidence$evidence != "Species-specific source evidence"]) == subtype_indirect(type))
  v
}
# number of the largest-ranged analysed parasites that belong to genus g (Appendix S5)
n_top_p <- function(g) {
  p <- main_table[main_table$interaction_type %in% "p", ]
  n <- sum(cumprod(p$genus[order(-p$range_area)] == g))
  stopifnot(n >= 2L)
  n
}
# omitting Phengaris raises the f-p and n-p ratios in all three models of Table S8 (Appendix S5)
stopifnot(all(vapply(c("lmm", "pgls_yumnam_2025", "pgls_schar_2018"), function(mo) all(vapply(c("f-p", "n-p"),
  function(ct) lg("Phengaris", mo, ct)$ratio > lg("none", mo, ct)$ratio, logical(1))), logical(1))))
# analysed parasites of model genus g that matched a tip of the tree rather than being grafted (Appendix S5);
# keyed on the model genus (Lycaena_ortygia is a Lepidochrysops)
n_matched_genus <- function(g, tree) {
  cw <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, paste0("crosswalk_", tree, ".csv")))
  sp <- main_table$species[main_table$genus %in% g & main_table$interaction_type %in% "p"]
  stopifnot(length(sp) == n_par_genus(g), all(sp %in% cw$analysis_species))
  sum(cw$matched[match(sp, cw$analysis_species)] %in% TRUE)
}
# origins of parasitism (Appendix S5): the Schar tree holds every analysed parasite; the four
# subfamilies are named in the text; Lepidochrysops and Thestor are one origin each on both trees; on the Yumnam
# tree Niphanda is absent and the two Ogyris parasites, one grafted, are separate origins
local({
  oc <- origin_clades
  stopifnot(orig("schar_2018")$n_parasites == cnt("model_area_type_p"),
            orig("yumnam_2025")$n_parasites < cnt("model_area_type_p"),
            all(origins$n_parasite_subfamilies[origins$tips == "grafted"] == 4L),
            setequal(unlist(strsplit(oc$subfamily, ";")), c("Aphnaeinae", "Miletinae", "Polyommatinae", "Theclinae")),
            all(table(oc$tree[oc$genera %in% c("Lepidochrysops", "Thestor")]) == 2L),
            !any(grepl("Niphanda", oc$genera[oc$tree == "yumnam_2025"])),
            sum(oc$tree == "yumnam_2025" & oc$genera == "Ogyris") == 2L,
            sum(oc$n_grafted[oc$tree == "yumnam_2025" & oc$genera == "Ogyris"]) == 1L,
            sum(oc$tree == "schar_2018" & oc$genera == "Ogyris") == 1L,
            orig("yumnam_2025", "matched")$changes < orig("schar_2018", "matched")$changes,
            orig("schar_2018", "matched")$changes < orig("schar_2018")$changes)
})
# parasitic genus-by-type units of the main type model and how many lie below the median facultative unit (Appendix S5)
gu_desc <- local({
  u <- aggregate(log10_range ~ genus + interaction_type, data = model.frame(main_models$area_type), FUN = mean)
  med_f <- median(u$log10_range[u$interaction_type == "f"])
  pu <- u[u$interaction_type == "p", ]
  pu <- pu[order(pu$log10_range), ]
  above <- paste0("*", as.character(pu$genus[pu$log10_range >= med_f]), "*")
  stopifnot(length(above) >= 2L)
  list(n_p = nrow(pu), n_f = sum(u$interaction_type == "f"), n_below = sum(pu$log10_range < med_f),
       above_txt = paste(paste(above[-length(above)], collapse = ", "), "and", above[length(above)]))
})
# one value shared by all main models of the given predictor sets (Table S3b caption)
meta_one <- function(column, predictors = c("type", "breadth")) {
  v <- unique(main_metadata[[column]][main_metadata$predictors %in% predictors])
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  v
}
# type-only LMM contrasts on the same side of p = 0.05 under log10 and Box-Cox (Appendix S3)
bc_lmm_type <- boxcox_comparison[boxcox_comparison$model == "lmm" & boxcox_comparison$predictors == "type", ]
# one range-area contrast of the type-only mixed model under both transformations
bc_row <- function(contrast) {
  d <- bc_lmm_type[bc_lmm_type$measure == "area" & gsub(" ", "", bc_lmm_type$contrast) == contrast, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  d
}
# the only contrast that changes side is the area facultative-mutualist contrast (supported under log10 only);
# the area mutualist-parasite contrast stays supported, with an interval above one
bc_same_side <- function() {
  same <- (bc_lmm_type$log_p < 0.05) == (bc_lmm_type$boxcox_p < 0.05)
  stopifnot(sum(!same) == 1L, bc_row("f-m")$log_p < 0.05, bc_row("f-m")$boxcox_p >= 0.05,
            bc_row("m-p")$boxcox_p < 0.05, bc_row("m-p")$boxcox_lower > 1)
  sum(same)
}
dataset_counts <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s02, "dataset_counts.csv"))
rec <- function(stage) {
  v <- dataset_counts$records[dataset_counts$stage == stage]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  v
}
# expert-polygon check of the outlier rule (s02_prepare_ranges, Outlier-rule check; Appendix S2): record groups flagged only by
# the stringent rule, and how many had centroids within 100 km of the expert polygon
og_check <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s02, "outlier_expert_check.csv"))
og_strict <- og_check[og_check$set == "strict only (f 0.25, not flagged at f 0.5)", ]
stopifnot(nrow(og_strict) == 1L)
og_strict_in <- round(og_strict$groups * og_strict$share_inside_expert)
stopifnot(abs(og_strict$groups * og_strict$share_inside_expert - og_strict_in) < 1e-6)
pg_geo <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "phylo_geography_contrasts.csv"))
pg_geo$contrast <- gsub(" ", "", pg_geo$contrast)
flip <- pg_geo$contrast == "n-f"
pg_geo$contrast[flip] <- "f-n"
pg_geo$ratio[flip] <- 1 / pg_geo$ratio[flip]
pg_moran <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s04, "phylo_geography_moran.csv"))
pgm <- function(model, study = "yumnam_2025") {
  v <- pg_moran$moran_500[pg_moran$model == model & pg_moran$study == study & pg_moran$measure == "area"]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  sub("-", "−", report_number(v, 2), fixed = TRUE) # true minus sign (U+2212), as in mor()
}
# Table S10 shows the phylogenetic spatial GAM. PGLS + butterfly background (also fitted in s04_fit_models, Joint phylogenetic and spatial models;
# residuals stay spatially autocorrelated) is a descriptive row of Table S12 (see robust above).
pg_geo <- pg_geo[pg_geo$model == "phylo_spatial_gam", ]
wing_coef <- read_report_table(file.path(dir_s06, "wingspan_coefficients.csv"))
# "ratio 1.98 per doubling of wingspan, 95% CI ..., p = ..." (type model; slope on log10 wingspan)
wing_txt <- function(measure = "area") {
  d <- wing_coef[wing_coef$measure == measure & wing_coef$predictors == "type", ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  dbl <- function(r) 2^log10(r) # ratio per tenfold wingspan -> per doubling
  sprintf("ratio %.2f per doubling of wingspan, 95%% CI %.2f–%.2f, %s", dbl(d$range_ratio), dbl(d$ratio_lower), dbl(d$ratio_upper), fmt_p(d$p_value))
}
cont <- function(type, column = "share_m_or_p") {
  v <- si_contamination[[column]][si_contamination$type == type]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1L)
  report_number(100 * v, 0)
}
# Appendix S6: log(1 + count) breadth "fitted all three range measures better" (lower ML AIC than the raw
# count for area, latitude and longitude), reported as the range of AIC differences, e.g. "3.7–4.1"; the
# type-adjusted obligate slope is "also positive"
breadth_daic <- local({
  sc <- check_table("breadth_scale_comparison")
  d <- sc$delta_AIC[sc$scale == "raw"]
  stopifnot(length(d) == 3L, all(d > 0), all(sc$delta_AIC[sc$scale == "log1p"] == 0))
  sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", min(d), max(d))
})
local({
  ob <- within_breadth[within_breadth$model == "lmm_obligate" & within_breadth$measure == "area", ]
  stopifnot(nrow(ob) == 1L, ob$ratio > 1)
})
# breadth with Paratrechina/Nylanderia merged into one count group (s05_check_robustness, Partner breadth; Appendix S6)
merge_eff <- function(model, measure = "area") {
  x <- check_table("breadth_genus_merge_effects")
  d <- x[x$model == model & x$measure == measure, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f per additional group, 95%% CI %.2f–%.2f, %s", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, fmt_p(d$p))
}
alt <- function(decision, contrast, measure = "area") {
  d <- si_alternative[si_alternative$decision == decision & si_alternative$contrast == contrast & si_alternative$measure == measure, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(d) == 1L)
  sprintf("ratio %.2f, %s", d$ratio, fmt_p(d$p))
}
# Appendix S6: for range area, f-p, n-p and breadth "remained supported under all four" codings, and f-m under all but
# the species-level-subtype coding
local({
  a <- si_alternative[si_alternative$measure == "area" & si_alternative$contrast %in% c("f-p", "n-p", "f-m", "breadth"), ]
  stopifnot(nrow(a) == 4L * length(unique(si_alternative$decision)), all(a$p[a$contrast != "f-m"] < 0.05),
            all(a$p[a$contrast == "f-m" & a$decision != "species_level_subtype_only"] < 0.05),
            a$p[a$contrast == "f-m" & a$decision == "species_level_subtype_only"] >= 0.05)
})
```

# Materials and Methods

## Ant-association data

To characterise larval ant associations across Lycaenidae, we compiled evidence
from regional and global syntheses [@eastwood1999; @heath2003; @fiedler2006;
@fiedler2012; @schar2018; @fiedler2021], the primary studies they cite and
further natural-history literature. Each of the
`r report_number(ledger_n("claims"))` claims from
`r report_number(ledger_n("sources"))` sources was recorded in an evidence
database with its source location and coding decision (Appendix S1). The first
author compiled the original data manually and then directed ChatGPT (OpenAI)
and Claude (Anthropic), which assisted literature discovery, extraction,
cross-checking and some classification decisions. As a consistency check, the resulting interaction
types agreed with the original manual
compilation for `r report_number(100 * legacy$share, 0)`% of shared species
(Cohen's kappa `r report_number(legacy$kappa, 2)`; Appendix S1). We matched
butterfly names to the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy and merged entries for the same
species into species units. Because the Backbone retains some outdated or
duplicate names, these units outnumber described species. Analysed genera
follow current checklists and phylogenies (Appendix S1).

We classified species into four interaction types: non-ant-associated (n),
facultatively associated (f), obligately mutualistic (m) and obligately
parasitic (p). Facultative associates can complete development without ants, but
obligate associates depend on them. Obligate mutualists obtain most of their
larval food independently of ants, whereas obligate parasites develop on ant
brood or other ant-derived food [@pierce2002]. An obligate species was assigned
to either subtype only when evidence on the species, or an explicit statement
about its genus, addressed larval feeding. We applied this rule equally to both
subtypes, so poorly known obligate species were not classified as mutualists by
default. We used inferences from relatives only when a source made them. Species
without interaction evidence remained unclassified and were not assumed to be
non-associated.

Ant-partner breadth was the number of ant genera, with names standardised across
sources, recorded attending or hosting the larvae or pupae of a species. We
excluded records marked as doubtful in their source, records of ant attacks or
mere co-occurrence, and ants identified only to subfamily (Appendix S1). Breadth
counts observed associations and does not measure experimentally established
compatibility.

## Occurrence data and range estimates

We used all `r report_number(rec("all_records_with_coordinates") / 1e6, 1)`
million Lycaenidae records with coordinates in a GBIF download from October 2026
[@gbif2026]. Because minimum convex polygons (MCPs) are sensitive to erroneous
and non-native records, we cleaned records with explicit
rules, without removing individual points by eye (Appendix S2). First, we
applied metadata and *CoordinateCleaner* filters [@zizka2019]. Second, we
removed documented introductions and records far from each species' native
region, defined by country checklists [@pinkert2022] or biogeographic realms
[@dinerstein2017]. Third, because a single misidentified or mislocated record can greatly
enlarge an MCP, we removed small outlying groups separated from the remaining localities
by more than both 200 km and a quarter of their maximum extent. We chose these
thresholds after an exploratory comparison with expert range polygons (Appendix S2).

We measured range area and the latitudinal and longitudinal extents of each
range, the north–south and east–west distances (km) spanned by its localities
(Appendix S2). Range area, the primary response, was the MCP area in a
species-specific equal-area projection, and the two extents served as
complementary measures. All three describe the extent of occurrence, which
includes unoccupied ground within the range [@gaston2009]. We analysed species
with at least ten unique cleaned localities, below which the cleaning protocol
flagged range estimates as data-poor. For the `r report_number(si_expert$n)`
European-centred species with expert range polygons [@hausharter2023], MCP and
expert polygon areas were closely correlated on a log~10~ scale (r =
`r report_number(si_expert$pearson_log10, 2)`; Appendix S2).

## Range-size models

For each range measure, we fitted a taxonomic linear mixed model of log~10~
range size with interaction type as a fixed effect and, to account for the
non-independence of related species, random intercepts for genus nested within
subfamily [*lme4* and *lmerTest*, @bates2015; @kuznetsova2015]. We used
taxonomic random effects because they cover all `r pgc("analysed")` analysed
species (Appendix S5), whereas only `r pgc("matched")`, including
`r report_number(pg("n_parasite", tree_set = "matched"))` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites, matched a tip of the time-calibrated
phylogeny of @yumnam2025, hereafter the Yumnam tree. We then fitted a second
model to ant-associated
species with recorded partners, adding mean-centred partner breadth to
interaction type. Breadth entered as an
untransformed count, so its coefficient gives the range-size ratio per
additional recorded ant genus. Recorded breadth varies mainly among facultative
species, so we also estimated the breadth association within them (Appendix
S6). Because the two models use different
species, we interpret the breadth association separately from the type
differences.

We report effects as ratios of fitted geometric-mean range sizes, back-transformed
from the log~10~ scale, with 95% confidence intervals. Geometric means are less
influenced than arithmetic means by a few very large ranges. Pairwise type
contrasts, all reported for the main models, used *emmeans* with
Tukey adjustment within each model [@lenth2026]. We describe effects with
p < 0.05 as supported or clear, without adjusting for the three range measures
or the sensitivity analyses. Because model-based intervals are also approximate
(Appendices S3–S5), inference rests instead on range area and on the consistency
and precision of estimates across complementary analyses.
Appendix S3 gives model diagnostics, R² [@barton2026] and a Box–Cox check of
sensitivity to the log transformation (Table S3c). Analyses were conducted in R
[@rcore2023].

## Sensitivity analyses

We tested robustness with `r num_word(length(core_analyses))` core analyses
(Fig. 4), each using the largest sample its method allowed (Appendices S2,
S4–S7). These were the reference taxonomic model; a spatial model;
species-level phylogenetic, joint spatial–phylogenetic and equal-weight
genus-level phylogenetic models, each on two trees; and models
of rarefied ranges
and of modelled ranges from @daru2024. Other analyses were additional checks.
The core analyses share data and are not independent replicates, so the number
supporting a contrast indicates consistency.

*Spatial structure.* To account for positive spatial autocorrelation in
taxonomic-model residuals [@dormann2007], we fitted spatial generalised additive
models (GAMs) with a spherical smooth of each species' range centre and
random-effect smooths for subfamily and genus [@wood2025].

*Shared ancestry.* We fitted phylogenetic generalised least squares (PGLS),
estimating Pagel's lambda [@pagel1999], on the Yumnam tree and, as an
alternative hypothesis, on the Schär tree, the COI topology of @schar2018 with
Grafen branch lengths [@grafen1989]. Unmatched species were grafted within their
genus, so their placement reflects taxonomy alone (matched-only PGLS in
Appendix S5). Species from genera absent from a tree were omitted, leaving
`r report_number(rb("pgls_grafted_yumnam_2025", "f-p")$n)` species on the Yumnam
tree.

*Space and ancestry combined.* PGLS residuals also remained spatially
autocorrelated, so we fitted joint GAMs combining the spherical smooth with a
phylogenetically structured species effect [@freckleton2009]. A spatial smooth
can absorb part of a genuine difference between geographically clustered
categories [@hodges2010], as can a phylogenetic effect for phylogenetically
clustered ones. We therefore treat the spatial and joint models as the most
conservative estimates, which need not recover the true difference.

*Concentration in a few lineages.* We counted origins of parasitism by
parsimony, fitted PGLS to equally weighted genus-by-interaction-type means and
refitted species-level models without
each major parasitic genus or the two largest together, and within and outside
southern Africa (Appendix S5).

*Occurrence sampling and range estimation.* We re-estimated ranges from equal
numbers of randomly drawn localities (rarefaction) and restricted analyses to
species with range estimates stable under subsampling at 90% [@gupta2020], 80%
or 95% thresholds. We also
compared cleaning treatments and used modelled native ranges from a global
butterfly database [@daru2024], which combine occurrences with environmental
data and include poorly recorded species (Appendices S2, S6).

*Further checks.* We separately added three covariates: wingspan, larval
carnivory (among non-parasites) and the regional butterfly background, the
average modelled range size of co-occurring butterflies of all families. We also
refitted the models with obligate species reclassified under alternative
codings (Appendices S4–S6).

# Results

## Data coverage and the geography of interaction strategies

Of the `r cnt("units")` species units, `r cnt("units_typed")` met the evidence
criteria for an interaction type. The `r cnt("model_area_type_total")` of these
that also met the criterion for an analysed range estimate (at least ten unique
cleaned localities), from `r cnt("model_genera")` genera, entered the main models
(`r cnt("model_area_type_n")` non-associated,
`r cnt("model_area_type_f")` facultative, `r cnt("model_area_type_m")`
obligately mutualistic and `r cnt("model_area_type_p")` obligately parasitic;
Table S2).

Interaction strategies showed distinct geographic patterns (Fig. 1). Facultative
and non-associated species occurred across major regions, whereas the recorded
obligate mutualists and parasites were confined to Afro-Eurasia and Australasia.
Parasites formed the highest proportions of classified species in southern Africa
(Fig. 1D), which also contained many small-ranged lycaenids (Fig. 1E), so
interaction strategy and range size shared geographic structure. Mean recorded
partner breadth varied among regions (Fig. 1F). Apparent regional absences
may partly reflect uneven recording and incomplete classification (Fig. S4).

```{r main-biogeography}
report_figure("plot_interaction_maps")
```

**Figure 1.** Global distribution of ant-interaction strategies, range size and
recorded partner breadth in Lycaenidae, in 500-km equal-area cells (Equal Earth
projection). A–D: proportions of classified species that were non-associated,
facultative, obligate mutualists and obligate parasites, in cells with at least
ten classified species. Each of these panels has its own square-root colour
scale, spanning the 1st to 99th percentiles of its cells (rounded outwards to
0.1), so colours are not comparable between panels; the few cells beyond this
range take the end colour (≤ or ≥ in the legend). E: median MCP area of species
with range estimates (logarithmic scale), in cells with at least ten such
species. F: mean number of recorded ant genera per ant-associated species
(linear scale), in cells with at least five associated species with recorded
breadth. Each species is counted once per occupied cell, using its stringently
cleaned records; grey land has no estimate. The maps describe the recorded
fauna; sampling and classification coverage are shown in Fig. S4.

## Interaction strategy and range size

We found that obligate parasites had the smallest fitted ranges (Fig. 2; Table
1). Facultative associates had `r ratio("lmm", "f-p")` times the estimated range
area of parasites (`r ci_p("lmm", "f-p")`), and non-associated species
`r ratio("lmm", "n-p")` times (`r ci_p("lmm", "n-p")`). Obligate mutualists were
intermediate, with smaller ranges than facultative associates and larger than
parasites (Table 1). Facultative associates had the largest point estimate, but
their difference from non-associated species was uncertain
(`r effi("lmm", "f-n")`). Interaction type accounted for
`r report_number(100 * main_metadata$marginal_r2[main_metadata$measure == "area" & main_metadata$predictors == "type"], 1)`%
of the variation in log~10~ range area (marginal R²; Table S3a).

The facultative–parasite and non-associated–parasite contrasts were also
supported for both range extents (Table 1). The mutualist–parasite contrast was
supported for
latitudinal but not longitudinal extent, and the facultative–mutualist contrast
for longitudinal but not latitudinal extent.

```{r main-type}
report_figure("plot_range_by_interaction_type")
```

**Figure 2.** Geographic range size by interaction type: A, MCP area; B,
latitudinal extent; C, longitudinal extent (logarithmic axes; n gives the number
of species). Coloured violins show the distribution of range sizes among the
analysed species of each type, all drawn with the same maximum width. White
boxes show medians and interquartile ranges, whiskers extend to the most extreme
values within 1.5 times the interquartile range of the box edges (on the log
scale), and small points show values beyond them. Black diamonds and bars show
the model-estimated geometric mean of each type with its 95% confidence interval
(back-transformed estimated marginal means of the taxonomic models, for a
typical genus and subfamily). These means can differ from the medians because
the log ranges of non-associated and facultative species have a long tail of
small values, and because the models attribute part of the small ranges of
species-rich genera (e.g. *Chrysoritis*, *Lepidochrysops*) to genus instead of
interaction type. Types sharing a letter do not differ clearly (Tukey-adjusted
p ≥ 0.05), which does not make them equivalent. Table 1 gives the ratios and
intervals.

**Table 1.** Range-size ratios in the main taxonomic models
(`r cnt("model_area_type_total")` species; breadth model:
`r cnt("model_area_breadth_n")`). Ratios compare the first category with the
second. Type contrasts have Tukey-adjusted 95% confidence intervals and
p-values; breadth has a coefficient-based interval and p-value and is the ratio
per additional recorded ant genus. n: non-associated; f: facultative; m:
obligate mutualist; p: obligate parasite. P-values below 0.05 are bold.
Appendix S3 gives model fit, estimated means and breadth-model type contrasts.
Spatial and phylogenetic models assess the non-independence left in these

```{r table-1-main}
t1_rows <- c(
  `f-p` = "f / p", `n-p` = "n / p", `m-p` = "m / p", `f-m` = "f / m", `f-n` = "f / n", `n-m` = "n / m",
  breadth = "Per recorded ant genus"
)
t1 <- data.frame(Contrast = unname(t1_rows), check.names = FALSE)
measure_names <- c(area = "Area", lat = "Latitudinal extent", lon = "Longitudinal extent")
for (key in names(measure_names)) {
  t1[[measure_names[[key]]]] <- vapply(names(t1_rows), function(k) {
    d <- rb("lmm", k, key)
    sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f) %s", d$ratio, d$lower, d$upper, format_table_p(d$p))
  }, "")
}
report_table(t1, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Recorded partner breadth and range size

Among the `r cnt("model_area_breadth_n")` ant-associated species with recorded
partners, range size increased with the number of recorded ant genera after
accounting for interaction type (Fig. 3; Table 1). Each additional genus was
associated with `r pct("lmm")` greater area, and both range extents also
increased with breadth. Facultative associates had more recorded partners than
mutualists and parasites (median `r num_word(breadth_med[["f"]])` versus
`r num_word(breadth_med[["m"]])` genus). The breadth association nevertheless
held among facultative species alone, with `r within_eff("lmm_facultative")`
greater area per additional genus, and remained after spatial adjustment (Table
S13a). Recorded breadth varied much less among obligate associates, and their
separate slope was imprecise (Appendix S6).

```{r main-breadth}
report_figure("plot_range_by_partner_breadth")
```

**Figure 3.** Range size against the number of recorded ant genera: A, MCP area;
B, latitudinal extent; C, longitudinal extent (logarithmic range axes). Points
are species, jittered horizontally so that species with the same number of
recorded genera remain visible. Lines and 95% confidence bands are fixed-effect
predictions of the taxonomic models, with a common breadth slope and
type-specific intercepts, drawn over the breadth values observed in each type
and dashed where fewer than five species of that type have at least that many
recorded genera. Breadth slopes within facultative and within obligate species
are reported in Appendix S6.

## Robustness to space, ancestry, lineages and range estimation

Facultative associates had clearly larger ranges than parasites in
`r core_support("f-p")` core analyses (Fig. 4; range-area ratios `r span("f-p")`),
and non-associated species in `r core_k("n-p")` (ratios
`r span_supported("n-p")`), all except the
Yumnam joint model (`r rp("phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025", "n-p")`). Residuals of
the taxonomic models were positively spatially autocorrelated (Moran's I =
`r mor("lmm", 500)` within 500 km; Table S6), so their intervals are probably
too narrow. Spatial adjustment removed this positive autocorrelation, leaving
weak negative autocorrelation (Moran's I = `r mor("spherical_gam", 500)`). It
also reduced the parasite contrasts, with the facultative–parasite ratio falling
from
`r ratio("lmm", "f-p")` (taxonomic model) to `r ratio("spherical_gam", "f-p")`
(spatial model). Phylogenetic adjustment alone changed this ratio less
(`r ratio("pgls_grafted_yumnam_2025", "f-p")` and
`r ratio("pgls_grafted_schar_2018", "f-p")` in species-level PGLS on the Yumnam
and Schär trees). Joint spatial and phylogenetic adjustment gave the most
conservative estimate, `r eff("phylo_spatial_yumnam_2025", "f-p")` on the Yumnam
tree.

The mutualist–parasite and facultative–mutualist contrasts kept their direction
in every core analysis but were supported in `r core_k("m-p")` and
`r core_k("f-m")` of the `r num_word(length(core_analyses))`, respectively, and
in none of the spatial or joint models. Obligate mutualists differed clearly
from non-associated species only in species-level PGLS on the Schär tree.
Facultative associates had larger point estimates than non-associated species in
every core analysis (Fig. S8), but clearly so only with the modelled ranges of
@daru2024. Partner breadth remained positively associated with range area in
every analysis estimating it (Table S12).

Parasites were concentrated in two genera, *Lepidochrysops*
(`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops")` species) and *Thestor*
(`r n_par_genus("Thestor")`). With genus-by-type units weighted equally,
facultative genera had larger ranges than parasitic genera on both trees,
including without *Lepidochrysops* (Table S9). Omitting any major parasitic
genus other than *Lepidochrysops* left both parasite contrasts supported in all three
species-level models (Table S8). The facultative–parasite contrast remained
supported in two of these three models without *Lepidochrysops*, outside
southern Africa and even without both genera, which contain
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops") + n_par_genus("Thestor")` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites. The exception was Yumnam-tree PGLS
(without *Lepidochrysops*, `r lg_rp("Lepidochrysops", "pgls_yumnam_2025")`;
Tables S8, S13c). The non-associated–parasite contrast was more sensitive. It
lost clear support without both genera (all three species-level models and
Yumnam genus-level PGLS), without *Lepidochrysops* (Yumnam-tree species- and
genus-level PGLS), outside southern Africa (taxonomic model and Yumnam-tree
PGLS) and in the 90% and 95% range-stability subsets (Tables S8, S9, S12, S13c).

Among species centred in southern Africa
(`r reg_row("southern_Africa_only")$n_parasite` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites), parasites had clearly smaller ranges
than facultative and non-associated species in the taxonomic model and in PGLS
on both trees. In the taxonomic model, facultative associates' ranges were about
`r report_number(reg_row("southern_Africa_only")$ratio, 0)` times those of
parasites (95% CI `r report_number(reg_row("southern_Africa_only")$lower, 1)`–`r report_number(reg_row("southern_Africa_only")$upper, 0)`).
Obligate mutualists there did not differ clearly
from parasites and had smaller ranges than facultative associates in all three
models (Table S13c). Species centred in Afro-Eurasia and Australasia, including
all analysed parasites, gave a facultative–parasite contrast similar to the
full-sample estimate (taxonomic model; Table S13c).

Facultative associates had clearly larger ranges than parasites under every
alternative range estimate.
Rarefied and full ranges of the same species gave similar ratios
(`r ratio("rarefied_k10", "f-p")` with ten localities against
`r ratio("lmm", "f-p")`; Table S13b). Parasites were disproportionately excluded
by the ten-locality threshold, but the modelled ranges [@daru2024], which relax this
threshold and include more parasites (Table S2), gave a smaller but supported
difference (`r rp("modelled_ranges_daru", "f-p")`). In the 80%, 90% and 95%
range-stability subsets the ratios were
`r report_number(rb("stability_80", "f-p")$ratio, 2)`,
`r report_number(rb("stability_90", "f-p")$ratio, 2)` and
`r report_number(rb("stability_95", "f-p")$ratio, 2)` (all supported, the last with
`r fmt_p(rb("stability_95", "f-p")$p)`; Table S12), although the 95% subset retained only
`r num_word(rb("stability_95", "f-p")$n_parasite)` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites.

Parasites also had clearly smaller ranges than facultative and non-associated
species under every alternative coding and cleaning, and in Box–Cox-transformed
taxonomic models (Tables S3c, S11, S14a), although inclusive cleaning and
requiring species-level subtype evidence each roughly halved the
facultative–parasite ratio, to `r halved_fp_span`. The mutualist–parasite
contrast lost support under both decisions and under the broader parasite
definition of @fiedler2012. The interaction and breadth associations
remained supported with wingspan as a covariate (Table S12; Appendix S6).

```{r main-robustness}
report_figure("plot_robustness_core_analyses")
```
