# Discussion

Contrasting interaction strategies showed a clear range-size signature in
Lycaenidae, but mainly at the parasitic end of the mutualism–parasitism
spectrum. In what is, to our knowledge, the first family-wide test, covering
`r cnt("model_area_type_total")` species, obligate parasites had smaller ranges
than facultative associates in every core analysis. Their contrast with
non-associated species held in all but the most conservative analysis, although
it was more sensitive to omitting parasitic genera or southern Africa. This
supports the expectation that parasites, which both depend on ants and exploit
them, have the smallest ranges (hypothesis 3), although they differed less
consistently from obligate mutualists. Obligate mutualists were intermediate,
and the smaller ranges expected from their dependence on compatible ants
received only weak, model-dependent support (hypothesis 2). Facultative
associates, expected to benefit from ants without depending on them (hypothesis
1), had larger ranges than parasites but rarely differed clearly from
non-associated species. Because they form the majority of ant-associated
species, coding ant association as present or absent would largely have hidden
this pattern. Recorded partner breadth covaried positively with range size,
consistent with the niche-breadth hypothesis (hypothesis 4). Range size thus
varied with how, rather than whether, species interact with ants.

Although interactions are often assumed to matter less for total range size than
for individual range boundaries [@paquette2021; @galiana2023], our results show
that interaction strategy can be associated with total range size. This
signature accounted for a modest share of variation, with interaction type alone
explaining
`r report_number(100 * main_metadata$marginal_r2[main_metadata$measure == "area" & main_metadata$predictors == "type"], 1)`%
of log~10~ range area and type and recorded breadth together
`r report_number(100 * main_metadata$marginal_r2[main_metadata$measure == "area" & main_metadata$predictors == "breadth"], 1)`%
among species with recorded partners (marginal R²; Table S3a). The association
is consistent with the suggestion that ant associations form an additional
niche dimension in Lycaenidae [@hausharter2023]. We could not include climatic,
habitat and plant-diet breadth as covariates, because comparable estimates
exist mainly for European-centred species, which include few obligate
associates, and occurrence-derived climatic breadth would partly reflect range
extent. Whether ant interactions act independently of these dimensions, and
whether they explain the negative plant-diet relationship within the family,
therefore remains to be tested.

## Obligate parasites have consistently small ranges

Several features of parasitism could explain why parasites have small ranges. Parasites must
be accepted by compatible colonies and exploit them [@pierce2002; @fiedler2012],
and among fleas, more host-specific species have smaller ranges [@krasnov2005].
In *Lepidochrysops* and *Phengaris* (= *Maculinea*), which include
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops") + n_par_genus("Phengaris")` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` analysed parasites, larvae first feed on plants
[@pierce2002], so food plants and compatible colonies must coincide. Small
ranges were not a general feature of carnivory. The
`r carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore` carnivorous non-parasites, mostly
hemipteran-feeding Miletinae, did not have smaller ranges than plant feeders,
although no analysed parasite was coded as a plant feeder, so carnivory cannot
be fully separated from parasitism (Appendix S6).

Constraints on local occupancy need not, however, produce a small extent of
occurrence [@gaston2009], as the best-studied parasites show. In European
*Phengaris*, dependence on particular *Myrmica* species was proposed to explain
why populations occupy few of the sites where their food plants and *Myrmica*
ants are abundant [@thomas1989]. Yet Palaearctic *Phengaris* have some of the
largest parasite ranges in our sample (Appendix S5), consistent with host use
that varies geographically, combining local specialisation with host sharing and
switching [@tartally2019].

Part of the parasite signal is geographic. Most analysed parasites occur in
southern Africa, where many lycaenids, particularly in the Cape, have small
ranges (Fig. 1D,E). After accounting for interaction type, the spatial model
also estimated smaller ranges in other regions, including West Africa,
Mediterranean-type regions, Madagascar and islands (Fig. S5). The parasite
contrasts shrank substantially under spatial and further under joint adjustment,
but this need not mean a weaker association, because a range-centre smooth
compresses each distribution to one location and can absorb part of a genuine
difference between geographically clustered strategies [@hodges2010].
Why interaction strategies are
geographically concentrated merits further research, and climate, ant
assemblages, habitat and evolutionary history may help explain it
[@pellissier2012; @piercedankowicz2022a].

Uneven sampling could also contribute, through which species are classified and
how well their ranges are recorded. Outside southern Africa, unclassified
species had smaller ranges than classified ones, whereas within southern Africa,
where most species are classified, the two differed less (Appendix S2).
Classified facultative and non-associated species elsewhere may therefore be
biased towards large ranges, inflating their contrasts with parasites. Yet
within southern Africa, parasites had clearly smaller ranges than both groups in
all three models, with larger ratios than in the full sample (Table S13c), so
uneven classification does not explain the contrast. Both parasite contrasts
also held with rarefied, modelled and differently cleaned ranges (Fig. 4;
Tables S13b, S14a), so the association does not depend on one way of estimating
ranges.

Species age offers an alternative explanation. *Lepidochrysops*, with
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops")` of the `r cnt("model_area_type_p")` analysed
parasites, diversified rapidly from about 6.5 million years ago, when its
phyto-predaceous life history probably evolved [@espeland2023]. Older species
tend to have larger ranges across many plant and animal groups [@alzate2025], so
if many parasites arose in recent radiations, their small ranges could partly
reflect their youth instead of ecological constraints of parasitism. Yet small
ranges were not confined to *Lepidochrysops*. Genus-level comparisons indicate
that they recur in several parasitic clades (Table S9; Fig. S7), and
two of the
three species-level models retained the facultative–parasite contrast without
*Lepidochrysops* (Table S8). Parsimony on both trees required at least
`r orig("schar_2018")$changes` origins of parasitism among the analysed species,
in `r num_word(orig("schar_2018")$n_parasite_subfamilies)` subfamilies
(Appendix S5), so the association is unlikely to rest on the few transitions
that can make comparative associations appear strong
[@maddison2015; @uyeda2018]. Because parasitism arose repeatedly, these
independent origins offer natural replicates for testing whether, and why,
ranges contracted afterwards, for example by combining dated
transitions with species ages, host-ant distributions and colony compatibility.

## Mutualistic associations show weaker range-size differences

Facultative associates rarely differed clearly from non-associated species,
giving limited support for the range-expanding benefits often reported for
facultative positive interactions [@stephan2021]. Local benefits of ant
attendance, such as better larval survival [@forister2010], need not translate
into larger ranges.

Obligate mutualists had intermediate ranges, compatible with partner dependence
constraining distributions while mutualistic benefits partly offset it
[@stephan2021; @fowler2022]. Because mutualists and parasites both depend on
ants, whereas only parasites exploit them, comparing the two could separate
dependence from exploitation. Parasites had smaller estimated ranges than
mutualists in every core analysis, clearly so in `r core_k("m-p")` (Fig. S8).
In southern Africa, however, where both obligate strategies are concentrated,
the two did not differ clearly, so it remains open whether small parasite ranges
reflect exploitation or obligate dependence. The mutualist contrasts were also sensitive to spatial adjustment,
genus weighting and the choice of phylogeny, and the mutualist–parasite contrast
lost support under
`r num_word(sum(si_alternative$decision != "main" & si_alternative$measure == "area" & si_alternative$contrast == "m-p" & si_alternative$p >= 0.05))`
of the `r num_word(length(setdiff(unique(si_alternative$decision), "main")))`
alternative codings. Shared habitat or lineage effects could produce the
intermediate pattern, so we treat the mutualist comparisons as secondary.

## Species with more recorded ant partners have larger ranges

Niche breadth is among the most consistent correlates of range size, but it is
usually measured through climate, habitat or diet [@slatyer2013]. Our results,
like those for trophic interactions in gall-inducing sawflies [@galiana2023],
suggest that the same pattern holds for the breadth of biotic partners. The
association held within facultative species and rests mainly
on them, because recorded partner counts vary little among obligate associates,
consistent with their much greater partner specificity [@fiedler2001]. A
log-transformed count fitted range area better than the raw count, suggesting
smaller proportional increases in range area with each additional recorded genus
(Appendix S6).

Because the association held in every analysis, including spatial, phylogenetic,
rarefied-range and modelled-range models (Table S12), it is unlikely to reflect only
regional ant diversity or research effort, shared ancestry or occurrence
sampling. Three processes could still produce it. First, using more ant genera
may let butterflies occupy more places, just as greater use of a widespread
host plant allowed the lycaenid *Aricia agestis* to expand its range
[@pateman2012]. Second, wide-ranging species encounter more potential partners
[@hurtado2024]. Among Lycaeninae, the ant genera associated with most butterfly
species are largely the most prevalent and widespread [@fiedler2001], so
widespread facultative species may accumulate partner genera simply by meeting
more ant assemblages. Third, better-studied butterflies may have more partner
records and better-recorded ranges. Rarefaction does not standardise partner
documentation, and claim counts, often repeated across syntheses, cannot measure
documentation effort. All three predict that few small-ranged species have many
recorded partner genera (Fig. 3).

Recorded breadth is also an imperfect measure of partner use. Larval attendance
does not show that an ant is a compatible or necessary partner throughout
the range, and for parasites a single recorded host genus can hide
geographically variable host specificity [@tartally2019]. Data on partner-ant
distributions and standardised field surveys of larval attendance would test
whether partner availability limits butterfly ranges
and whether recorded breadth reflects encounter opportunity or biological
flexibility.

# Conclusions

Lycaenid range size varied with how, rather than whether, species interact with
ants. Obligate parasites, which arose at least `r orig("schar_2018")$changes`
times, consistently had the smallest ranges, and species with more recorded
partner genera had larger ranges. Comparative explanations of range size have
centred on climatic, habitat and resource niches; our results suggest that the
type of biotic interaction belongs alongside them. Testing whether other
partner-dependent clades show a similar pattern, strongest where interactions
become parasitic, would reveal how generally the biotic niche is reflected in
range size.

## Appendix S1. Ant-association data

**Evidence database.** Every interaction claim was recorded as one row of an
evidence database linking the species as published, the source, the page, table
or row, the claim (interaction category, ant association, documented
non-association, carnivory) and, for ant records, the ant taxon and the kind of
association. The database contains `r report_number(ledger_n("claims"))` claims
from `r report_number(ledger_n("sources"))` sources for
`r report_number(ledger_n("species"))` species. Sources were syntheses for Australia [@eastwood1999], southern Africa
[@heath2003], the Palaearctic [@fiedler2006], ant-parasitic species
[@fiedler2012] and the family as a whole [@schar2018; @fiedler2021], together
with the primary studies they cite, regional encyclopaedias and further
species-level literature. Disagreements between sources were kept in the
database, and the chosen value and its reasoning were recorded in a decision register.

**Names.** All butterfly names were matched to the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy
through a synonym database. GBIF keys representing one biological species under
an older and a modern genus combination were merged into a single species,
whereas different species that share an epithet, author and year (for example
*Pentila inconspicua* and *Triclema inconspicua*, which belong to different
subfamilies) were kept separate. Metalmarks (Riodinidae) that the GBIF Backbone
lists within Lycaenidae were excluded. The resulting `r cnt("units")` species
units link evidence to occurrence records. They outnumber the almost 5,400
described species [@pierce2002; @piercedankowicz2022a] because the GBIF
Backbone, assembled from many source checklists, still accepts some outdated or
duplicate names that could not all be identified and merged. The count is
therefore not an estimate of species richness. Ant names were matched to currently accepted genera.

**Genus classification.** Species identities and names follow the GBIF Backbone,
which links the interaction data to the occurrence records, but the genus used
in the models (random effects, subfamily assignment, grafting onto the
phylogenies) was updated where the Backbone retains outdated combinations. Two
kinds of change were made. First, genus names treated as junior synonyms or
subgenera in current classifications were merged with their senior genus:
*Agrodiaetus* and *Plebicula* with *Polyommatus*, *Lycaeides* with *Plebejus*,
*Everes* with *Cupido*, the Palaearctic copper segregates (*Helleia*,
*Palaeochrysophanus*, *Thersamonia*, *Loweia*) with *Lycaena* and other
Palaearctic cases following @wiemers2018; *Maculinea* with *Phengaris*
[@fric2007]; *Poecilmitis* and *Oxychaeta* with *Chrysoritis* [@heath1997];
*Spindasis* with *Cigaritis* [@boyle2015]; Nearctic subgenera of *Callophrys*
and *Satyrium* following @pelham2008; and *Epamera*, *Argiolaus* and
*Trichiolaus* with *Iolaus* [@larsen2005]. Second, species placed in a genus to
which they do not belong were moved to their current genus when this was
supported by the names used in the modelled range maps [@daru2024] or in the
published phylogenies [@schar2018; @kawahara2023; @yumnam2025], together with
regional checklists [@robbins2004; @pelham2008; @wiemers2018; @warren2024boa].
Examples are American hairstreaks still combined with the Palaearctic genus
*Thecla*, *Lycaena ortygia* (= *Lepidochrysops ortygia*), *Lycaena arionides*
and *Glaucopsyche alcon* (= *Phengaris*), *Thestor callimachus* (= *Tomares
callimachus*, a Palaearctic theclinine previously assigned to the African
parasitic genus *Thestor*) and *Lepidochrysops ariadne* and *Euchrysops niobe*
(= *Orachrysops*). Genera that current phylogenies continue to recognise (for
example *Lysandra*, *Kretania*, *Agriades* and *Tharsalea*) were kept. The
revision changed the genus of `r cnt("model_genus_revised")` analysed species
and no interaction type; each change, its evidence and its source are listed in
the genus revision table of the repository.

**Interaction type.** Facultative associates are attended by ants but can
complete development without them, whereas obligate associates depend on ants.
Obligate associates were divided by the source of larval food. A species was
classified as an obligate parasite when its larvae develop on food obtained from
ants, by preying on ant brood or eggs or by being fed by ants in place of plant
food. It was classified as an obligate mutualist when its larvae feed on plants
or other non-ant food, such as algae, while attended by ants, even if ants
occasionally regurgitate food to them. Larvae that prey on ant-tended
hemipterans, such as aphids and scale insects, also obtain their own food and
were not classified as parasites. When sources disagreed, we used the type
recorded by more independent sources; ties went to direct observations of the
species over reviews and compilations, and then to the more recent source.
Inferences from relatives were used only for species without direct evidence.
For this reason,
*Axiocerses harpax* and two *Crudaria* species, which @schar2018 treated as
mutualists, were classified as parasites, because their larvae were observed
feeding on ant-derived food in ant runs (*A. harpax*) or shown not to eat plants
(*Crudaria*; Table S11). Scores that their authors marked as doubtful, records
of no ant association in @schar2018 and parasite records resting only on ants
regurgitating food to larvae were used only when a species had no other
evidence.

**Evidence criteria for the analysis.** We analysed interaction types that a
source stated for the species, based on observations or on the source's own
assessment of the species, or for the whole genus (for example, that all species of a genus are parasites). Types
that could only be inferred from relatives by our own rules were not used. For
obligate species, the mutualist or parasite subtype also needed evidence on
larval food, with the same standard for both subtypes. This evidence was a
source classifying the species as mutualistic or parasitic from its biology, a
larval feeding category (herbivorous or entomophagous) in @heath2003, or an
explicit genus statement, such as that older larvae of *Thestor* feed on ant
brood or that *Orachrysops* larvae are not parasites of ants [@fiedler2012].
Obligate species whose subtype had merely been assumed (for example, "mutualist,
because no parasitism has been recorded"), or whose genus statement established
only obligate association, were left unclassified. Most of them were southern
African Aphnaeinae such as *Aloeides*, whose larvae live in ant nests and whose
genus includes both herbivorous species and a documented egg predator (*A.
pallida*).

For `r subtype_indirect("p")` of the `r cnt("model_area_type_p")` analysed
parasites (mainly *Lepidochrysops* and *Thestor*) and
`r subtype_indirect("m")` of the `r cnt("model_area_type_m")` mutualists, the
subtype did not come from a species-level classification in the source that
documented the obligate association. For
`r subtype_indirect("p") - subtype_added("p")` of these parasites and
`r num_word(subtype_indirect("m") - subtype_added("m"))` mutualists, both the
association and the subtype rested on a genus statement or a source's inference
from relatives. For the other `r num_word(subtype_added("p"))` parasites and
`r subtype_added("m")` mutualists, the obligate association was documented for
the species, but the subtype came from separate evidence on larval food or from
a genus statement, so Table S1 counts them as species-specific. Appendix S6
reports the models without all of these species, and Table S1 gives the
evidence basis of the analysed types.

**Ant-partner breadth.** Breadth was the number of ant genera recorded
attending, visiting or hosting the larvae or pupae of a species, or tending the
hemipterans on which its larvae feed. We excluded
records that sources marked as doubtful, ants attacking larvae and other
aberrant associations, co-occurrence only, laboratory-only records, visits to
adults or eggs, and ants identified only to subfamily. We counted genera
because many sources do not identify ants to species [@fiedler2012]. For
parasites, a recorded genus need not be one in whose nests the larva can
complete development, so breadth measures documented association, which can
exceed the range of hosts that support development. Old *Paratrechina* records
that cannot be assigned to *Paratrechina* or *Nylanderia* formed one count
group alongside resolved records of either genus, so counts approximate the
number of present-day genera; merging all three into one group gave a similar
association (Appendix S6). In Table 19 of @fiedler1991, a question mark before
an ant species epithet marks an uncertain species identification within a known
genus, and these records were kept, whereas a question mark after the epithet
can mark a doubtful record, and these were excluded. A source correction
register in the repository lists these exclusions and the attack record for
*Ogyris genoveva* and, where an excluded record's genus was still counted, the
other records that support it. The reported breadth models use the corrected counts, and the
corrections left interaction types and range estimates unchanged.

**Use of AI tools.** The interaction data were first compiled manually by the
first author. The rebuilt dataset was then extended with the help of ChatGPT
(OpenAI) and Claude (Anthropic) in 2024–2026, which helped to locate, extract
and cross-check literature records and to make some classification decisions under the
first author's direction. The decision register records whether each decision was
taken by the first author or with AI assistance, and the database links each
retained claim to its source location. Not every extraction was independently
checked a second time. Of the `r report_number(legacy$shared)` species
entries of the manual compilation that had one of the four interaction types in
both compilations, `r report_number(legacy$agree)`
(`r report_number(100 * legacy$share, 0)`%) received the same type in the
rebuilt dataset (Cohen's kappa `r report_number(legacy$kappa, 2)`). The two
compilations draw largely on the same syntheses, and the rebuild was
cross-checked against the earlier coding, so this agreement measures the consistency
of coding.

**Table S1.** Evidence basis of the interaction types of the species in the main
models. Species-specific source evidence includes both observations and
statements in compilations, so not every entry is an independent field
observation. Species without interaction evidence were left unclassified.

```{r table-s1-evidence}
ev <- si_evidence[, c("evidence", intersect(c("n", "f", "m", "p"), names(si_evidence)), "total")]
# rows from the most to the least direct evidence; the middle category is the source's own inference from
# relatives for the named species (interaction_type_basis 'presumed_relatives', not genus-level; s06_summarise_results, Supporting Information tables)
ev_labels <- c(`Species-specific source evidence` = "Species-specific source evidence",
  `Stated for the species in a source (no direct observation)` =
    "Presumed for the species in a source (the source's inference from relatives; no direct observation)",
  `Genus-wide presumption stated in a source` = "Genus-wide presumption stated in a source")
stopifnot(setequal(ev$evidence, names(ev_labels)))
ev <- ev[match(names(ev_labels), ev$evidence), ]
ev$evidence <- unname(ev_labels[ev$evidence])
names(ev) <- c("Evidence", "Non-associated", "Facultative", "Mutualist", "Parasite", "Total")[seq_len(ncol(ev))]
report_table(ev, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Appendix S2. Occurrence data and range estimates

**Download and names.** We used all Lycaenidae records with coordinates in a
GBIF download from October 2026 [@gbif2026]
(`r report_number(rec("all_records_with_coordinates"))` records), interpreted
with the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy so that names matched the interaction data.
Records of subspecies were assigned to their species. Records that GBIF had
resolved only above species rank were assigned to a species when their verbatim
name exactly matched an accepted species or a reviewed synonym; no fuzzy
matching was used.

**Record filters.** Fossil and living-specimen records, records explicitly
described as introduced, records dated before 1900, records with more than 1,000
individuals and records with coordinate uncertainty above 25 km were excluded;
records without stated uncertainty were retained if both coordinates had at
least two decimal places. *CoordinateCleaner* [@zizka2019] flagged zero and
equal coordinates, country and province centroids, biodiversity institutions,
the GBIF headquarters, records at sea (with a 10-km coastal buffer) and records
near capital cities (within 1 km, or within 10 km when imprecise). After these
filters `r report_number(rec("base_main"))` records remained.

**Native region and introductions.** Country checklists of @pinkert2022 were
mapped onto GADM country boundaries and RESOLVE biogeographic realms
[@dinerstein2017]. For species whose records broadly agreed with their checklist
(at least 80% of occupied 25-km cells within 300 km of listed countries),
records more than 300 km from the listed countries were removed. For species
without a reliable checklist, realms holding at least 10% of a species' cells or
at least two cell–dataset incidences were taken as native, and records more than
300 km from them were removed. A cell–dataset incidence counts each dataset once
per occupied cell, so a single dataset recorded in two cells of a realm
scores two. Nine documented introductions and four cases in which GBIF names
combine different species concepts on different continents were removed with
explicit geographic rules, each supported by a cited source
(`r report_number(rec("introduced_removed"))` records).

**Geographic outliers.** Remaining localities were thinned to one per 25-km cell
and grouped by single-linkage clustering of great-circle distances. A group was
removed if it contained at most 10% of the species' localities (or two
localities, whichever was larger) and was separated
from the remaining localities by a gap exceeding both 200 km and one-quarter of
their maximum great-circle extent. The rule was applied iteratively and never
reduced a species below five localities. We chose this stringent treatment
after an exploratory comparison with expert range polygons. The intermediate
treatment used gaps of 250 km and half the remaining extent,
retained groups supported by multiple datasets and had a more permissive
native-region rule. An inclusive treatment retained flagged geographic outliers.
All three were evaluated in identical-species as well as eligible-species models
(Table S14a), keeping interaction coding fixed. The facultative–parasite area
contrast persisted; mutualist–parasite contrasts were less consistent. The final
stringent dataset contained `r report_number(rec("final_strict_plus"))` records.

**Thinning and range measures.** Species spanning more than 250 km were thinned
to one record per approximately 50-km Equal Earth cell, all species were thinned
to a 10-km minimum great-circle distance, and minimum-convex-polygon vertices
were restored, so that thinning removed redundant interior records without
changing the range boundary. Latitudinal extent is the north–south distance (km)
between the northernmost and southernmost localities. Longitudinal extent is the
occupied east–west span: longitudes are treated as a circle, so that ranges
crossing the 180° meridian are not split, the span is 360° minus the largest
longitude gap without localities, and it is converted to kilometres along the
parallel midway between the latitudinal limits. Area is
the planar MCP in a species-specific cylindrical equal-area projection whose
seam lies in the largest empty longitude gap, so that ranges crossing the
antimeridian are continuous. Species with fewer than ten unique localities, the
threshold at which the cleaning protocol flags a range estimate as data-poor,
were not analysed (Table S2). Fig. 2 shows the range sizes of all analysed
species by interaction type.

**Comparison with expert ranges.** For the `r report_number(si_expert$n)`
European-centred species with expert range polygons [@hausharter2023], MCP and
expert polygon areas were closely correlated on a log~10~ scale (r =
`r report_number(si_expert$pearson_log10, 2)`; Fig. S1). MCP areas were on
average `r report_number(si_expert$geometric_ratio, 2)` times the expert areas,
as expected because convex hulls include unoccupied ground. On these species,
the stringent cleaning matched the expert polygons slightly better than the
other treatments (Table S14b), but the same species guided the choice of
cleaning, so this is not an independent validation. The stringent outlier rule
can also remove plausibly genuine disjunct populations: of the
`r report_number(og_strict$groups)` record groups that only this rule removed,
`r report_number(og_strict_in)` had centroids within 100 km of the expert
polygon.

**Stability of range estimates.** To measure how much each range estimate
depends on its particular records, we followed @gupta2020, who treated an
estimate as complete when the last 20% of records added less than 10% to it. We
drew 1,000 random subsamples of 80% of each species' thinned localities and
divided their mean range estimate by the full estimate. Because removing
records can only shrink a convex hull or an extent, this ratio is at most one.
Estimates with ratios above 0.9, which meet this criterion, were treated as
stable, and a looser threshold of 0.8 and a stricter one of 0.95 bracket it
(Fig. S2; Appendix S6).

**Classification coverage.** Interaction types are known for a larger share of
species in southern Africa, where most parasites occur, than elsewhere, and this
could bias the comparison with parasites. Outside southern Africa (defined by
range centre; Appendix S5),
`r report_number(100 * cov_row("elsewhere")$share_classified, 0)`% of species
with a range estimate had an analysed interaction type, and their geometric
mean range area was
`r report_number(signif(cov_row("elsewhere")$gm_area_classified, 2))` km²,
against `r report_number(signif(cov_row("elsewhere")$gm_area_unclassified, 2))`
km² for unclassified species. In southern Africa, which holds
`r cov_row("southern_Africa")$parasites` of the `r cnt("model_area_type_p")`
analysed parasites,
`r report_number(100 * cov_row("southern_Africa")$share_classified, 0)`% were
classified, and classified and unclassified species had more similar ranges
(`r report_number(signif(cov_row("southern_Africa")$gm_area_classified, 2))`
and `r report_number(signif(cov_row("southern_Africa")$gm_area_unclassified, 2))`
km²). Most facultative and non-associated species occur outside southern
Africa, so as a group they may be biased towards wide-ranging species, which
would inflate their contrasts with parasites. The comparison within southern
Africa, where most species are classified, tests this (Table S13c; Appendix
S5).

**Modelled ranges.** As an alternative method of range estimation, we repeated
the taxonomic models with the native range maps of @daru2024, estimated through
species distribution modelling with occurrence-derived alpha hulls and
environmental and habitat information. These maps relax our cleaning and
locality requirements and include poorly recorded species
(`r report_number(daru_parasites)` parasites, against
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` with occurrence-based ranges; Table S2). They draw
on the same public occurrence sources, so they test the method of range
estimation on largely the same records.

**Table S2.** Species with an interaction type that met the evidence criteria,
with a range estimate from at least ten unique localities, in the main type and
breadth models, and with a modelled range [@daru2024], by interaction type.

```{r table-s2-attrition}
att <- si_attrition
att$interaction_type <- c(n = "Non-associated", f = "Facultative", m = "Mutualist", p = "Parasite")[att$interaction_type]
names(att) <- c("Interaction type", "Classified", "Range (≥ 10 localities)", "Type model", "Breadth model", "Modelled range")
report_table(att, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r figure-s1, out.width=if (knitr::is_html_output()) '60%' else '3.9in'}
report_figure("plot_expert_validation")
```

**Figure S1.** Occurrence-based minimum-convex-polygon area against expert
range-polygon area for `r report_number(si_expert$n)` European-centred species
[@hausharter2023], on logarithmic axes. The grey line is one-to-one, and the blue
line and band are a least-squares fit and its 95% confidence band.

```{r figure-s2}
report_figure("plot_accumulation_example")
```

**Figure S2.** Range-size accumulation curves for *Celastrina argiolus*: A,
latitudinal extent; B, longitudinal extent; C, range area. Each of 1,000 random
permutations of the species' thinned localities was accumulated in steps of 50
localities; black lines show means and grey ribbons one standard deviation.
Longitudinal extent is the occupied circular span converted to east–west
distance at the midpoint latitude of the full range, and area is the planar MCP
in the species-specific cylindrical equal-area projection of the full set of
localities. Because the seam, reference latitude and projection stay fixed, the
curves cannot decline as localities are added. The range-stability criterion
(Appendix S2) compares the mean of 80% subsamples with the full estimate.

## Appendix S3. Main taxonomic mixed models

The main taxonomic mixed models are summarised in Table 1 and Fig. 2 of the
main text. Table S3a gives their fit and the tests of interaction type and
partner breadth, Table S3b their variance components, Table S3c a comparison
with Box–Cox-transformed responses, Table S4 the back-transformed estimated
marginal means and Table S5 the pairwise contrasts in the models with partner
breadth (those of the type models are in Table 1).

```{r table-main}
main_tables <- publication_log_model_sections(main_models, main, main_means, main_metadata)
```

**Table S3a.** Model fit and hypothesis tests for interaction type and
ant-partner breadth as predictors of log~10~ geographic range size. Mixed models
include genus nested within subfamily as random effects; sample sizes are given
in the model labels. Area is the primary response; Lat and Lon are latitudinal
and longitudinal extent. R²m and R²c are marginal and conditional R². Breadth
ratio is the multiplicative change in expected range per additional recorded ant
genus, with 95% confidence interval. P-values smaller than 0.05 are bold.

```{r table-s3-fit}
report_table(main_tables$fit,
  align = c("l", "l", rep("r", ncol(main_tables$fit) - 2L)),
  escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
```

**Table S3b.** Variance components of the primary taxonomic models on the log~10~
response scale. Subfamily and genus are random-intercept variances; residual is
the residual variance. Singularity indicates a boundary variance estimate. All
models contain `r num_word(meta_one("subfamilies"))` subfamilies; the type
models contain `r meta_one("genera", "type")` genera and the breadth models
`r meta_one("genera", "breadth")`.

```{r table-s3b-variance}
v3 <- main_metadata
v3 <- v3[order(match(v3$measure, c("area", "lat", "lon")), match(v3$predictors, c("type", "breadth"))), ]
report_table(data.frame(
  Model = ifelse(v3$predictors == "type", "Type", "Type + breadth"),
  Metric = c(area = "Area", lat = "Lat", lon = "Lon")[v3$measure], N = v3$n,
  Subfamily = sprintf("%.3f", v3$subfamily_variance), Genus = sprintf("%.3f", v3$genus_variance),
  Residual = sprintf("%.3f", v3$residual_variance), Singular = ifelse(v3$singular, "Yes", "No"),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE)
```

**Response transformation.** To check whether the results depend on the
log~10~ transformation, we refitted the main models with Box–Cox-transformed
responses [@box1964]: the three type-only mixed models, the range-area mixed
model with breadth and the two range-area joint models on the Yumnam tree, each
with the same species, predictors and covariance structure. Each power was
chosen by maximising the likelihood of the full-sample mixed model, including
the Jacobian of the transformation: `r bc_power_text("area_type")`,
`r bc_power_text("lat_type")` and `r bc_power_text("lon_type")` for area,
latitudinal and longitudinal extent in the type-only models and
`r bc_power_text("area_breadth")` for area with breadth. The joint models used
the corresponding area powers. The transformation was
$[(y/g)^\lambda-1]/\lambda$, where $g$ is the geometric mean of the sample.
Box–Cox effects are not constant ratios, so we report ratios of back-transformed
predictions, which depend on the reference prediction, with delta-method
intervals that treat the power as known. Type contrasts kept the Tukey
adjustment, and breadth tests apply to the coefficient on the transformed scale.

**Table S3c.** Range-size ratios under log~10~ and Box–Cox transformation of
the response. LMM: taxonomic mixed model; Joint: phylogenetic spatial GAM on the
Yumnam tree; N in brackets. Each cell gives the ratio (95% interval) and p.
Contrasts in the breadth models are evaluated at one recorded ant genus, and
joint-model predictions set the spatial and phylogenetic effects to zero. Ant
genus compares one with two recorded genera in facultative species. Box–Cox
intervals are approximate and can disagree with the test when p is close to
0.05. n: non-associated; f: facultative; m: mutualist; p: parasite. P-values
below 0.05 are bold.

::: {.allow-page-break}
```{r table-s3c-boxcox}
bc3 <- boxcox_comparison
stopifnot(nrow(bc3) == 29L,
          !anyDuplicated(bc3[c("model", "measure", "predictors", "contrast")]))
# show non-associated / facultative as f / n, as in Table 1 and Table S12: reciprocal ratios with
# swapped bounds; p-values unchanged
bc_flip <- bc3$contrast == "n - f"
stopifnot(sum(bc_flip) == 4L)
for (s in c("log", "boxcox")) {
  r <- paste0(s, "_ratio"); lo <- paste0(s, "_lower"); up <- paste0(s, "_upper")
  old_lo <- bc3[[lo]][bc_flip]
  bc3[[r]][bc_flip] <- 1 / bc3[[r]][bc_flip]
  bc3[[lo]][bc_flip] <- 1 / bc3[[up]][bc_flip]
  bc3[[up]][bc_flip] <- 1 / old_lo
}
bc3$contrast[bc_flip] <- "f - n"
bc_cell <- function(ratio, lower, upper, p) {
  sprintf("%.2f (%.2f–%.2f) %s", ratio, lower, upper, format_table_p(p))
}
model_label <- paste0(
  ifelse(bc3$model == "lmm", "LMM", "Joint"),
  ifelse(bc3$predictors == "type", ": type", ": breadth"),
  " (", bc3$n, ")"
)
metric_label <- unname(c(area = "Area", lat = "Lat", lon = "Lon")[bc3$measure])
group <- paste(model_label, metric_label)
first <- !duplicated(group)
report_table(data.frame(
  `Model (N)` = ifelse(first, model_label, ""),
  Metric = ifelse(first, metric_label, ""),
  Effect = ifelse(bc3$contrast == "breadth", "Ant genus",
                  gsub(" - ", " / ", bc3$contrast, fixed = TRUE)),
  `Log10 ratio (95% CI); p` = bc_cell(bc3$log_ratio, bc3$log_lower,
                                  bc3$log_upper, bc3$log_p),
  `Box–Cox ratio (95% CI); p` = bc_cell(bc3$boxcox_ratio, bc3$boxcox_lower,
                                    bc3$boxcox_upper, bc3$boxcox_p),
  check.names = FALSE
), align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
```
:::

The main results held under Box–Cox. The facultative–parasite contrast and the
breadth association remained supported, including in the joint models, and
`r bc_same_side()` of the `r nrow(bc_lmm_type)` contrasts of the type-only mixed models stayed on the
same side of p = 0.05. The exception was the area facultative–mutualist
contrast (`r fmt_p(bc_row("f-m")$log_p)` under log~10~ and `r fmt_p(bc_row("f-m")$boxcox_p)` under
Box–Cox). The area mutualist–parasite contrast of the type-only model remained
supported (Box–Cox ratio `r report_number(bc_row("m-p")$boxcox_ratio, 2)`, 95% CI
`r sprintf("%.2f–%.2f", bc_row("m-p")$boxcox_lower, bc_row("m-p")$boxcox_upper)`). Box–Cox made the residuals of the
taxonomic models nearly symmetric, but those of the joint models were still
skewed and heavy-tailed, and a transformation does not address spatial
dependence. We kept log~10~ as the primary transformation because it gives
constant, directly interpretable range ratios, and fixed-effect estimates of
mixed models are generally unbiased, although less precise, when distributional
assumptions are violated [@schielzeth2020].

**Table S4.** Back-transformed estimated marginal means and 95% confidence
intervals for the models in Table S3a. Area is in millions of km²; latitude and
longitude are in km. Breadth-model means are evaluated at one recorded ant
genus.

```{r table-s4-estimates}
report_table(main_tables$estimates,
  align = c("l", "l", rep("r", ncol(main_tables$estimates) - 2L)),
  escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r table-pairwise}
main_contrast_table <- publication_log_contrast_table(contrasts)
```

**Table S5.** Pairwise differences between the estimated range sizes of the
three ant-associated types in the models with partner breadth; the contrasts of
the type models are given in Table 1. Ratios greater than one indicate that the
first category has the larger expected range. f: facultatively associated; m:
obligately mutualistic; p: obligately parasitic. Confidence intervals and
p-values are Tukey-adjusted across the three contrasts in each breadth model.
P-values smaller than 0.05 are bold.

```{r table-s5-pairwise}
s5 <- main_contrast_table[main_contrast_table$Model == "Type + breadth", setdiff(names(main_contrast_table), "Model")]
stopifnot(nrow(s5) == 9L)
report_table(s5, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"), escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
```


**Model diagnostics and inference.** No main taxonomic model was singular
(Table S3b), and Fig. S3 shows the spread and tails of the residuals. Type
contrasts used Kenward–Roger degrees of freedom (*emmeans* and *pbkrtest*;
@lenth2026; @halekoh2014), and omnibus and breadth tests in the mixed models
used Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. In the spatial models, type contrasts
used normal approximations and breadth tests the GAM summary. PGLS intervals
treat the fitted lambda and the tree as known, so they include no uncertainty
in graft placement or phylogeny. Heavy residual tails and the spatial
autocorrelation of the taxonomic residuals (Table S6) make nominal intervals and
p-values approximate, which is why we compared estimates across covariance
structures (Table S12) and response transformations (Table S3c).

```{r figure-s3-diagnostics}
report_figure("plot_model_diagnostics")
```

**Figure S3.** Residual diagnostics of the range-area models. Rows, from top:
taxonomic and spherical spatial type models, then taxonomic and spherical
spatial breadth models. Left: normal quantile–quantile plots; right: residuals
against fitted log~10~ area, with a smoothed trend. Spatial dependence is shown
in Table S6.

## Appendix S4. Geographic analyses

**Spatial patterns.** Fig. S4 maps, in 500-km equal-area cells, the number of
recorded species and the proportions of them with an interaction type and with
a range estimate. Small ranges and parasites are both concentrated in the
south-western Cape (Fig. 1D,E), so interaction-type differences could partly
reflect geography, which the spatial models address. Classification is least
complete, and species counts most variable, in the tropical Americas and
central Africa (Fig. S4A,B), so the proportion maps of Fig. 1 mask cells with
fewer than ten classified species.

**Spherical GAM.** Each species was represented by the spherical centroid of its
occupied 200-km Equal Earth cells, or by a spherical medoid when opposite parts
of a very broad distribution made the centroid unstable. Centres and the
butterfly background were computed from the records of the intermediate
cleaning, whereas range measures and maps used the stringent cleaning. Models
contained interaction type (or type and partner breadth), a spline on the
sphere of latitude and longitude (basis dimension 160) and random-effect smooths
for subfamily and genus, fitted by REML with *mgcv* [@wood2025]. These models
estimate differences among interaction types at a given location. Because a
spatial smooth can also absorb part of a genuine difference between
geographically clustered categories [@hodges2010], they may understate these
differences. The fitted spatial surface (Fig. S5) shows larger expected ranges at high northern latitudes and in continental
interiors, and smaller ranges in the Cape and on the south-eastern coast of
southern Africa, in West Africa, Mediterranean-type regions, temperate South
America, Madagascar and on islands.

**Regional butterfly background.** We also asked whether a species' range is
small relative to the butterflies living in the same regions.
For each 500-km Equal Earth cell occupied by a species, we averaged the log~10~
modelled range areas [@daru2024] of all butterfly species of every family in
that cell, excluding the species' own genus and requiring at least five
comparison species, and averaged these cell values with equal weight over the
species' occupied cells (Fig. S6). This background entered the mixed models as
a centred covariate. We used butterflies of all families as comparators because
co-occurring lycaenids share the trait under test: the co-occurring lycaenids
of a parasite were on average `r cont("p")`% obligate mutualists or parasites,
compared with `r cont("f")`% for a facultative species and `r cont("n")`% for a
non-associated species, so a lycaenid background would partly adjust for
interaction type itself. Relative to this background, facultative associates had
`r ratio("background_500km_butterflies", "f-p")` times and non-associated
species `r ratio("background_500km_butterflies", "n-p")` times the range area of
parasites (Table S12). The background can itself share geographic structure with
interaction types, and its residuals remained spatially autocorrelated, so we
treat it as a descriptive check with less weight than the spherical GAM.

**Residual spatial autocorrelation.** We measured Moran's I of model residuals
among species whose range centres lay within 500 km or 1,000 km of each other
(Table S6). Residuals of the taxonomic mixed models were positively
autocorrelated (Moran's I = `r mor("lmm", 500)` within 500 km), as were those
of the models with the butterfly background, so their intervals are probably
too narrow. The spherical GAM removed this positive autocorrelation and left
weak negative autocorrelation (Moran's I = `r mor("spherical_gam", 500)`).

```{r figure-s4}
report_figure("plot_richness_range_maps")
```

**Table S6.** Residual spatial autocorrelation in the range-area type models:
Moran's I of residuals among species whose range centres lie within 500 km (and
1,000 km for the full-sample models), with binary distance weights. The expected
value under no autocorrelation is close to zero (−1/(N − 1)). For the
phylogenetic models (Appendix S5), Moran's I was computed at 500 km only and
without a test (–); raw PGLS residuals retain the phylogenetic covariance,
whereas normalised residuals have it removed. P-values smaller than 0.05 are
bold.

```{r table-s6-moran}
m1 <- data.frame(
  Model = c(
    lmm = "Taxonomic mixed model (main)", background_500km_butterflies = "Mixed model + butterfly regional background",
    spherical_gam = "Spherical spatial GAM"
  )[moran$model],
  `Distance (km)` = moran$distance_km, N = moran$n, `Moran's I` = sprintf("%.3f", moran$moran_i),
  p = format_table_p(moran$p), check.names = FALSE
)
pm <- pg_moran[pg_moran$measure == "area", ]
pm_models <- c(
  pgls_raw_residuals = "PGLS, raw residuals", pgls_normalised_residuals = "PGLS, normalised residuals",
  pgls_background_normalised_residuals = "PGLS + butterfly background, normalised residuals",
  phylo_spatial_gam = "Phylogenetic spatial GAM"
)
pm <- pm[pm$model %in% names(pm_models), ]
pm <- pm[order(match(pm$model, names(pm_models)), match(pm$study, c("yumnam_2025", "schar_2018"))), ]
m2 <- data.frame(
  Model = paste0(
    pm_models[pm$model], " (",
    c(yumnam_2025 = "Yumnam", schar_2018 = "Schär")[pm$study], ")"
  ),
  `Distance (km)` = 500, N = pm$n, `Moran's I` = sprintf("%.3f", pm$moran_500), p = "–", check.names = FALSE
)
report_table(rbind(m1, m2), escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Appendix S5. Phylogenetic and lineage analyses

**Trees and matching.** We used two published phylogenies as alternative
hypotheses: the time-calibrated Lycaenidae phylogeny of @yumnam2025, used for
the main phylogenetic analyses, and the COI topology of @schar2018. Yumnam
branch lengths were used as published; Schär's substitution lengths, which
measure sequence divergence rather than time, were replaced by Grafen branch
lengths [@grafen1989] on the pruned topology before grafting. We did not analyse
the dated butterfly phylogeny of @kawahara2023 separately: Yumnam and
Kodandaramaiah used it as a constrained backbone, so these would share backbone
information. Species were matched to tips by identical names or unambiguous GBIF
accepted keys; fuzzy and ambiguous matches were excluded. Figure S7 shows the
interaction types and range areas of the matched species on the Yumnam tree;
parasitism occurs in several separate clades.

**Grafting.** Only `r pgc("matched")` of the `r pgc("analysed")` analysed
species matched a tip of the Yumnam tree (`r pgc("matched", "schar_2018")` for
Schär), and the matched species included only
`r report_number(pg("n_parasite", tree_set = "matched"))` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites; tree coverage is biased towards
well-studied lineages, so PGLS on matched species alone would test a smaller and
unrepresentative sample. We therefore grafted each analysed species missing from
a tree onto its genus. A species whose genus was represented by two or more tips
was attached to the most recent common ancestor of its congeners, forming a
polytomy at the genus node; a species with a single congener on the tree became
its sister, splitting that tip's branch at its midpoint. New branches kept the
trees ultrametric, and species of genera absent from a tree were omitted.
Grafting places species by taxonomy alone. It adds no sequence or
divergence-time information, leaves relationships among grafted congeners
unresolved and assumes that genera are monophyletic; where a genus is not, the
species was attached to the smallest clade containing all its congeners.
Grafting added `r pgc("grafted")` species to the Yumnam tree (`r pgc("on_tree")`
species on the tree) and `r pgc("grafted", "schar_2018")` to the Schär tree
(`r pgc("on_tree", "schar_2018")`).

**Species-level PGLS.** PGLS models had the same fixed effects as the mixed
models and estimated Pagel's lambda over 0–1 by profiling the likelihood
[@pagel1999] (Table S7). On the alternative Schär tree, the parasite contrasts
and the breadth association were supported as on the Yumnam tree, with larger
contrasts (facultative / parasite range area
`r effi("pgls_grafted_schar_2018", "f-p")`; Table S12).

**Influence of individual parasitic genera.** Parasites were concentrated in a
few genera, and *Lepidochrysops* and *Thestor* alone contributed
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops") + n_par_genus("Thestor")` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` analysed parasites. We therefore refitted the
species-level range-area models after omitting each parasitic genus with at
least three analysed parasites
(`r paste0("*", logo_single, "*", collapse = ", ")`), one at a time (Table S8).
In the mixed model and in PGLS on the Schär tree, the
facultative–parasite and non-associated–parasite contrasts remained supported in
every refit. On the Yumnam tree, both remained supported when any genus other
than *Lepidochrysops* was omitted, but not without *Lepidochrysops*, whose
species make up nearly half of the parasites. All but
`r num_word(n_matched_genus("Lepidochrysops", "yumnam_2025"))` of its
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops")` analysed species (all but
`r num_word(n_matched_genus("Lepidochrysops", "schar_2018"))` on the Schär tree)
were grafted, so their relationships within the genus were not resolved. The
mutualist–parasite contrast was the least robust: it was not supported in any of
the three models without *Lepidochrysops*, and in the mixed model it lost
support when `r num_word(n_mp_lost)` of the `r num_word(length(logo_single))`
genera were omitted individually. Omitting *Phengaris*, whose species include
the `r num_word(n_top_p("Phengaris"))` largest-ranged analysed parasites, raised
the estimated facultative–parasite and non-associated–parasite ratios in all
three models (Table S8).

**Genus-level PGLS.** Species-level PGLS gives every species a vote, so a
species-rich genus can dominate it. To ask instead whether small ranges recur
across parasitic lineages, we fitted PGLS at genus level. Each combination of
genus and interaction type was one unit (a genus with species of two types gave
two units), with the mean log~10~ range of its species in the main mixed-model
sample as the response. The tree was the genus-grafted tree pruned to one
species per unit, choosing the alphabetically first originally matched species
within each unit when available and otherwise the alphabetically first grafted
species. Multiple type units within a genus kept separate representative tips,
so the covariance still depends on which species represent a genus. Genera
absent from a tree were omitted, leaving `r gl("yumnam_2025")$n_units` units,
`r gl("yumnam_2025")$n_p_units` of them parasitic genera, on the Yumnam tree and
`r gl("schar_2018")$n_units` (`r gl("schar_2018")$n_p_units`) on the Schär tree
(Table S9). Parasitic genera had markedly smaller ranges than facultative genera
on both trees, with all genera and without *Lepidochrysops* (range area on the
Yumnam tree: `r gli("yumnam_2025")`; without *Lepidochrysops*:
`r gli("yumnam_2025", "Lepidochrysops")`). Descriptively, `r gu_desc$n_below` of
the `r gu_desc$n_p` parasitic genus-by-type units of the main mixed-model sample
(before omitting genera absent from a tree) had mean log~10~ range areas below the
median of the `r gu_desc$n_f` facultative units; the exceptions were
`r gu_desc$above_txt`. The facultative–parasite latitudinal contrast also
retained support on both trees with and without *Lepidochrysops*. For range area,
non-associated genera had larger ranges than parasitic genera on the Schär tree with and
without *Lepidochrysops*, and on the Yumnam tree with all genera but not without
*Lepidochrysops*. For range area, the mutualist–parasite and facultative–mutualist contrasts
were supported only on the Schär tree. Residual phylogenetic covariance among genus units was weak
(lambda `r report_number(gl("yumnam_2025")$lambda, 2)` on the Yumnam tree and
close to zero on the Schär tree, where the model is therefore close to an
ordinary comparison of genus means; Table S9).

**Origins of parasitism.** Associations resting on a few evolutionary
transitions can appear strong in comparative tests [@maddison2015; @uyeda2018],
so we counted how often parasitism must have arisen among the analysed species.
We coded each species of the main range-area sample as parasitic or not and
reconstructed this character by parsimony on the genus-grafted Yumnam and Schär
trees. Gains and losses had equal costs, the root was set as non-parasitic and
polytomies could be resolved in whichever way required the fewest changes. Both
trees required `r orig("schar_2018")$changes` changes, and no equally
parsimonious reconstruction included a loss of parasitism, so all were origins.
On the Schär tree, which includes every analysed parasite, the origins lay in
`r num_word(orig("schar_2018")$n_parasite_subfamilies)` subfamilies (Aphnaeinae,
Miletinae, Polyommatinae and Theclinae), and
`r num_word(length(origin_singles))` of them were single analysed species
(`r paste0("*", origin_singles, "*", collapse = ", ")`), each resting on the
classification of one species. On the Yumnam tree, which lacks
*Niphanda*, the two parasitic *Ogyris* species, one of them grafted, formed
separate origins, so the count was the same. With grafted species removed,
`r orig("yumnam_2025", "matched")$n_parasites` and
`r orig("schar_2018", "matched")$n_parasites` parasites remained on the Yumnam and Schär trees,
and parsimony required `r orig("yumnam_2025", "matched")$changes` origins on the
Yumnam tree and `r orig("schar_2018", "matched")$changes` on the Schär tree.
Parsimony gives the fewest origins compatible with a tree, and the count also
depends on the placement of grafted species, which reflects taxonomy alone.
*Lepidochrysops* and *Thestor*, each a single origin, contain
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops") + n_par_genus("Thestor")` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` analysed parasites (see *Sample and regional
concentration* below).

**Space and ancestry combined.** Phylogenetic adjustment alone left the
residuals spatially autocorrelated (Moran's I within 500 km =
`r pgm("pgls_normalised_residuals")` for the normalised PGLS residuals on the
Yumnam tree; Table S6), so we combined both adjustments in a phylogenetic
spatial GAM on the genus-grafted Yumnam and Schär trees (Table S10). It
contained a spherical spline (basis dimension 100), a species random effect
whose covariance followed the phylogeny (with an estimated variance instead of a
profiled Pagel's lambda) and an independent residual. Its residuals showed weak
negative autocorrelation within 500 km (Moran's I =
`r pgm("phylo_spatial_gam")` on the Yumnam tree; Table S6). The
facultative–parasite contrast and the breadth association remained supported
for all three range measures on both trees, and the non-associated–parasite
contrast for latitudinal extent on both trees and for all three measures on the
Schär tree. The contrasts involving mutualists kept their direction but were not
supported. Because lineage, region and interaction type overlap, this model
cannot show which of them accounts for the weaker contrasts. As a second
combination of phylogenetic and geographic adjustment, PGLS on both trees
included the regional butterfly background (Appendix S4) as a covariate. It
retained the facultative–parasite and non-associated–parasite area contrasts on
both trees (Table S12), but its residuals remained spatially autocorrelated (Moran's
I = `r pgm("pgls_background_normalised_residuals")` on the Yumnam tree; Table
S6), so we treat it as descriptive.

**Matched species, lineages and regions.** Three further tests asked whether the
parasite contrasts depend on grafted species, on the two largest parasitic
genera or on southern Africa (Table S13c). First, with tree-matched species
only, PGLS supported the facultative–parasite range area contrast on both
trees; the non-associated–parasite contrast pointed the same way (ratios
`r report_number(mcv("pgls", "n-p", "yumnam_2025")$range_ratio, 1)` and
`r report_number(mcv("pgls", "n-p", "schar_2018")$range_ratio, 1)` on the Yumnam and Schär trees) but
was not supported (`r fmt_p(mcv("pgls", "n-p", "yumnam_2025")$p.value)` and
`r fmt_p(mcv("pgls", "n-p", "schar_2018")$p.value)`), whereas the taxonomic model of the same species
supported both. The facultative–parasite contrast therefore does not require
the grafted species. Second, without
*Lepidochrysops* and *Thestor*, which contain
`r n_par_genus("Lepidochrysops") + n_par_genus("Thestor")` of the
`r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites, the facultative–parasite contrast
remained supported in the taxonomic model, in PGLS on the Schär tree and in
genus-by-type PGLS on both trees, but not in species-level PGLS on the Yumnam
tree. The non-associated–parasite contrast was more sensitive and remained
supported only in genus-by-type PGLS on the Schär tree. Third, among species
centred in southern Africa, parasites had smaller ranges than facultative and
non-associated species in the taxonomic model and in PGLS on both trees, with
wide intervals. Mutualists there also had smaller ranges than facultative
species and did not differ clearly from parasites. Outside southern Africa, the
facultative–parasite contrast remained supported in the taxonomic model and on
the Schär tree but not on the Yumnam tree, and the non-associated–parasite
contrast only on the Schär tree. Regions were assigned by range centre: southern
Africa as latitude < −15° and longitude 10–55° E, and Afro-Eurasia and
Australasia as east of 30° W (longitude ≥ −30°). These are coarse divisions, and most parasites of the southern African subset belong to
*Lepidochrysops* and *Thestor*.

## Appendix S6. Robustness to data decisions and covariates

**Range stability.** Restricting the models to species with stable range
estimates, at the 90% threshold of @gupta2020 or at the looser 80% and stricter
95% thresholds (Appendix S2), removed proportionally more parasites. Stability was assessed separately for each range
measure, so samples differ among measures; for range area,
`r rb("stability_80", "f-p")$n_parasite`,
`r rb("stability_90", "f-p")$n_parasite` and
`r rb("stability_95", "f-p")$n_parasite` of the `r cnt("model_area_type_p")`
parasites remained (Table S12). The area facultative–parasite ratio was
`r eff("stability_80", "f-p")` at 80%, `r eff("stability_90", "f-p")` at 90%
and `r eff("stability_95", "f-p")` at 95%. The 95% subset reduced the precision
of the area contrasts involving parasites, and the area non-associated–parasite
contrast lost clear support at 90% and 95% (Table S12). These criteria measure
how much an estimate depends on the observed localities, not how completely the
true distribution was sampled.

**Balanced occurrence samples.** We estimated ranges from 200 random draws of
ten or twenty cleaned localities per species, and from ten distinct occupied
25-km cells, each contributing one sampled locality. All draws used the full
range's longitude seam, equal-area projection and reference latitude, and the
response was the geometric mean of the replicate estimates. Models of the full
ranges of exactly the same species (Table S13b) separate the effect of sampling
from that of sample composition. The cell-based sample excludes species with
fewer than ten occupied cells. Intervals treat the averaged rarefied estimates
as fixed. These comparisons test the effect of locality number and clustering,
but they cannot recover unrecorded parts of a range.

**Breadth within strategies and functional form.** The breadth association held
within facultative species, with `r within_eff("lmm_facultative")` greater area
per additional recorded ant genus in the taxonomic model and
`r within_eff("spherical_gam_facultative")` after spatial adjustment (Table
S13a). Among obligate species, the type-adjusted slope was also positive but
imprecise, with `r within_eff("lmm_obligate")` greater area per genus. Parasites had only one or two
recorded genera each, too few for a separate slope. Slopes did not differ
clearly among the three associated types (likelihood-ratio test,
`r fmt_p(check_table("breadth_interaction_test")[["Pr(>Chisq)"]][2])`). A
log(1 + count) predictor fitted all three range measures better than the raw
count (AIC lower by `r breadth_daic`; Table S13d), suggesting that each
additional genus brings a smaller proportional increase in range size as breadth
grows. We kept the
raw count in the main models because it gives a ratio per recorded genus. Few
species have many recorded genera, so the shape of the relationship at high
breadth is uncertain. Merging historical *Paratrechina* records with resolved
*Paratrechina* and *Nylanderia* records into one count group per butterfly gave
a similar area association (`r merge_eff("lmm_pooled")`; facultative species:
`r merge_eff("lmm_facultative")`).

**Wingspan.** Larger butterflies may disperse farther, and wingspan has been
examined as a correlate of range size in butterflies [@hausharter2023]. We
therefore added log~10~ wingspan as a centred covariate to the main mixed models
for the `r cnt("model_wingspan_n")` analysed species with a measured wingspan
(values imputed from congeners were not used). Species with larger wingspans had
larger ranges (`r wing_txt("area")`), and the interaction and breadth
associations persisted (Table S12).

**Larval carnivory.** A species was coded as carnivorous when any source in the
evidence database recorded its larvae feeding on animal matter (ant brood, food
provided by ants or hemipterans) and as a plant feeder when sources recorded
only plant feeding. Species without such a record took the code shared by at
least 90% of at least three directly coded congeners, and remaining parasites of
brood-predator genera were coded as carnivorous. In the main range-area sample,
`r carn_n("p", "animal")` of the `r cnt("model_area_type_p")` parasites were
coded as carnivorous (`r carn_n("p", "animal", "genus")` from these genus
rules), the other `r num_word(carn_n("p", "uncoded"))` were uncoded and none
was coded as a plant feeder. Carnivory and parasitism therefore cannot be
separated in the interaction-type model. We instead asked whether carnivorous
species that are not ant parasites also had small ranges, by adding carnivory
to the main taxonomic model of the `r carn_row("coded")$n` non-parasites with a
carnivory code (`r carn_n(c("n", "f", "m"), "plant", "genus")` of their
plant-feeder codes came from congeners). The `r carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore`
carnivores comprised `r num_word(carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore_n)`
non-associated, `r num_word(carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore_f)` facultative and
`r num_word(carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore_m)` mutualistic species from
`r carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore_genera` genera, and
`r carn_row("coded")$n_carnivore_miletinae` of them were hemipteran-feeding
Miletinae. Their ranges did not differ clearly from those of plant feeders, and
the point estimate indicated larger carnivore ranges (raw geometric mean area
`r report_number(carn_row("coded")$geomean_carnivore / 1e6, 2)` versus
`r report_number(carn_row("coded")$geomean_plant / 1e6, 2)` million km²;
plant-feeder/carnivore `r carn_eff("coded")`). Results were similar for
latitudinal (`r carn_eff("coded", "lat")`) and longitudinal extent
(`r carn_eff("coded", "lon")`), when the
`r carn_row("uncoded_as_plant")$n - carn_row("coded")$n` uncoded non-parasites
were treated as plant feeders (`r carn_eff("uncoded_as_plant")`) and when
carnivores were limited to the `r carn_row("consistent_evidence")$n_carnivore`
species coded as such by at least two sources and as plant feeders by none
(`r carn_eff("consistent_evidence")`). Without Miletinae, only
`r num_word(carn_row("without_miletinae")$n_carnivore)` carnivores remained
(`r carn_eff("without_miletinae")`). The carnivores are few and concentrated in
one subfamily, which contains no plant feeders, so this comparison has little
power and wide intervals. It indicates only that small ranges are not shared by
all lycaenids with carnivorous larvae, and it cannot separate brood predation
from feeding by ants.

**Alternative classification decisions.** We refitted the main model under four
alternative codings of mutualists and parasites (Table S11). For range area, the
contrasts of parasites with facultative and non-associated species and the
breadth association remained supported under all four, and the
facultative–mutualist contrast under all but the coding that used only
species-level subtype evidence (`r alt("species_level_subtype_only", "f-m")`). The mutualist–parasite contrast was the most sensitive. Counting
as mutualists the obligate species whose subtype had only been assumed, mostly
small-ranged southern African Aphnaeinae, strengthened the
facultative–mutualist contrast and weakened the mutualist–parasite contrast.
Following @schar2018 in treating the three ant-fed aphnaeines of Appendix S1 as
mutualists slightly strengthened the mutualist–parasite and
facultative–parasite contrasts; this moved
`r num_word(alt_n("ant_fed_aphnaeines_as_m", "n_m") - alt_n("main", "n_m"))`
analysed species, because *Crudaria wykehami* has too few localities for a range
estimate. Two codings weakened the parasite contrasts and left the
mutualist–parasite area contrast unsupported. Using only subtypes coded directly
from the classifying source (Appendix S1) left
`r alt_n("species_level_subtype_only", "n_p")` parasites and
`r alt_n("species_level_subtype_only", "n_m")` mutualists (mutualist/parasite
`r alt("species_level_subtype_only", "m-p")`), and coding as parasites all
species that @fiedler2012 lists as ant parasites, a definition that includes
any recorded trophallaxis, gave `r alt_n("fiedler2012_parasites", "n_p")`
parasites (mutualist/parasite `r alt("fiedler2012_parasites", "m-p")`).

**Table S11.** Main taxonomic mixed model under alternative classification
decisions (range area and latitudinal extent). *Main*: the classification used
throughout. *Assumed subtype as mutualist*: obligate species whose mutualistic
or parasitic status had been assumed rather than documented are counted as
mutualists. This alternative also leaves unclassified *Thestor murrayi*, a
parasite in the main classification whose only species-level evidence is an
ant-attendance record. *Ant-fed aphnaeines as mutualists*: *Axiocerses harpax*,
*Crudaria capensis* and *C. wykehami* (no range estimate) classified as
mutualists, following @schar2018. *Species-level subtype only*: obligate species
whose mutualist or parasite subtype was not coded directly from the classifying
source (Appendix S1) are left unclassified. *Fiedler (2012) parasites*:
classified species that @fiedler2012 lists as ant parasites, a definition that
includes any recorded trophallaxis, are coded as parasites. N: species, with
mutualists/parasites in brackets. Ratios with Tukey-adjusted p-values; breadth
is per additional ant genus. P-values smaller than 0.05 are bold.

```{r table-s11-alternative}
options(report_table_width = 6.5) # Appendix S6 is portrait
eff7 <- c(`f-p` = "f / p", `n-p` = "n / p", `m-p` = "m / p", `f-m` = "f / m", breadth = "Ant genus")
a7 <- si_alternative[si_alternative$contrast %in% names(eff7), ]
a7$cell <- sprintf("%.2f %s", a7$ratio, format_table_p(a7$p))
labels7 <- c(main = "Main", assumed_subtype_as_m = "Assumed subtype as mutualist",
  ant_fed_aphnaeines_as_m = "Ant-fed aphnaeines as mutualists",
  species_level_subtype_only = "Species-level subtype only", fiedler2012_parasites = "Fiedler (2012) parasites")
stopifnot(setequal(unique(si_alternative$decision), names(labels7)))
# 'Assumed subtype as mutualist' is fitted on the earlier MAIN table, which leaves Thestor murrayi unclassified (caption)
stopifnot(alt_n("main", "n_p") - alt_n("assumed_subtype_as_m", "n_p") == 1L)
keys7 <- expand.grid(measure = c("area", "lat"), decision = names(labels7), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
t7 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(keys7)), function(i) {
  x <- a7[a7$decision == keys7$decision[i] & a7$measure == keys7$measure[i], ]
  n <- x$n[x$contrast == "f-p"][1]
  stopifnot(n == alt_n(keys7$decision[i], "n"))
  out <- data.frame(
    Classification = labels7[[keys7$decision[i]]],
    Metric = c(area = "Area", lat = "Lat")[[keys7$measure[i]]],
    N = sprintf("%d (%d/%d)", n, alt_n(keys7$decision[i], "n_m"), alt_n(keys7$decision[i], "n_p")),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
  for (e in names(eff7)) out[[eff7[[e]]]] <- x$cell[match(e, x$contrast)]
  out
}))
report_table(t7, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Appendix S7. Core and additional sensitivity results

This appendix collects the sensitivity results: the core analyses of Fig. 4 and
`r num_word(length(setdiff(names(analysis_labels), core_analyses)))` further
checks (Fig. S8, Table S12), and the targeted comparisons of breadth,
occurrence sampling, lineage and regional concentration, and cleaning (Tables
S13–S14). The taxonomic model of all species is the common reference, and the
spatial and joint models are treated as the most conservative estimates
(Materials and Methods). The analyses share data, so the three range measures,
the two trees and the alternative specifications are not independent
replicates.
